title: Private Road Agreements That Save Rural Closings
one_liner: A flat-fee e-sign-and-record service that produces the road-maintenance and shared-well agreements lenders demand, then turns each road into a dues-collecting association.
customer: Listing and buyer agents and title/escrow officers in rural and mountain markets (CO, MT, ID, WA, OR, UT, NC/TN mountains, northern New England) pay $400-750 per transaction. Later, the households on each road pay $15-40 a month through the association.
problem: A house on a private road often has no enforceable maintenance agreement, only a handshake among neighbors. FHA, VA, USDA and most conventional underwriters want a recorded, legally enforceable agreement, and similar paper for shared wells, septics and driveways. The appraiser flags the private road and the problem lands on nobody. It surfaces 7-10 days before closing, the neighbors have no reason to cooperate, and the deal slips or dies. Between sales the road decays because nobody can collect dues.
solution: Software plus templated law. (1) Detect private vs public roads from county GIS and identify every benefiting parcel and owner. (2) Use state-specific agreement templates reviewed once by local counsel. (3) Run a multi-party e-sign, remote online notarization and e-recording workflow with a friendly neighbor-outreach script. (4) Add a lender-ready cover letter that answers the standard underwriting condition. (5) Upsell to a formal road association (entity, EIN, bank account, ACH dues billing, reserve tracking, lien rights where state statute allows) and shared well/septic agreements.
why_now: Affordability pushes buyers toward exurban and rural homes, and many of them rely on FHA, VA or USDA financing with strict access rules. Remote online notarization and e-recording are now legal and routine in most states. Counties are refusing to accept new roads into public maintenance. Wildfire-zone insurers and fire districts increasingly care about year-round road access and maintenance.
revenue_model: $495 flat per agreement package, paid by the seller through escrow or by a title partner, plus pass-through recording fees. $250 add-on per shared well, septic or easement agreement. Recurring: $29/month association software plus a payment fee on dues (about 3% + $3 per household per month). Referral fees from title partners.
non_obvious_insight: The road is not the deal-killer. The 4-30 neighbors who each have zero incentive to sign are. So the product is the neighbor-consent workflow, not the document. The other insider fact is that underwriters usually accept a simple recorded agreement signed by a majority of owners with proportional cost shares. You don't need a full HOA. Once a road has bank-account-backed dues, it becomes a sticky recurring customer that nobody else serves.
first_30_days: Pick 2 counties dense with private roads (for example the foothills of Larimer/Boulder CO, or Flathead MT). Pull active listings and cross-match them to county road-class GIS to find listings on private roads. Pay a local real-estate attorney about $2-3k to review one template. Cold-contact those listing agents with a specific message: your listing is on a private road, the lender will ask for this, and we deliver in 7 days. Sign 5 pilots at $495 and 2 title officers as referral partners.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: PayHOA, Other small-HOA software (Buildium, AppFolio, HOA Start, Vantaca, Cinc and similar), Local real-estate attorneys and title/escrow companies (the incumbent workaround), Generic legal-form sellers (LegalZoom, US Legal Forms, Rocket Lawyer). White space: Only partly verified: the WebSearch budget (200/200) was exhausted before I could run any searches, so I could not check for a funded startup, Product Hunt or YC listing, or forum demand. I used direct page fetches and a GitHub search instead. What I found: (1) No direct competitor turned up in direct fetches, and GitHub has no open-source project for this. (2) The per-deal neighbor-consent workflow (identify benefiting parcels from county GIS, outreach script, multi-party RON/e-sign, e-record, lender cover letter) appears unserved by software. Today it is handled by attorneys and title officers by hand, with generic templates from form sellers. (3) The recurring association layer is NOT white space. PayHOA serves 0-25 unit associations at $49/mo with $2.45 flat ACH, against the idea's $29/mo plus 3% + $3 per household (about $3.45-4.20 on a $15-40 dues payment), so the idea's layer costs more per household than the incumbent. (4) The lender-demand premise is weaker than stated. The HUD Handbook 4000.1 text I could read (2019 edition, p.184 and p.566 of the PDF) requires private streets to be protected by a permanent recorded easement, ownership interest, or HOA ownership, says shared driveways do NOT require a joint maintenance agreement, and only has the appraiser ask whether a maintenance agreement exists and comment on road condition. So for FHA the real deal-killer is a missing recorded easement (a title/access cure), not the maintenance agreement. I did not verify VA, USDA or conventional rules or any newer HUD revision. The defensible unserved wedge is a title-partner-distributed neighbor-consent and recording workflow for lenders and loan types that do require the agreement, plus an easement/access cure.

title: Day-Zero Payoff Bridge for Floorplan Dealers
one_liner: Invert the radar: instead of catching dealers who fail to pay the floorplan lender, wire the payoff directly to the lender the day the car sells and get repaid when the retail contract funds, turning sold-out-of-trust risk into a short, fully secured receivable with data-driven underwriting.
customer: Independent and franchised dealers that sell through third-party indirect finance and get squeezed when contracts in transit, stips or unwinds stretch funding beyond the floorplan payoff window. Pilot referral partners are two or three independent floorplan lenders. Capital comes from a credit fund or family-office vehicle buying short-dated receivables. Dealer pays a per-deal fee, and the floorplan lender shares in it and saves audit cost and risk.
problem: SOT often starts as a timing gap, not fraud. The dealer has delivered the car, the retail lender has not yet funded, and the floorplan payoff clock is running. That is why honest and dishonest dealers look identical in the books for a week or more, and it is how a small cash squeeze becomes fraud. Detection tools (including the parent) only tell the lender after the timing gap has already turned into a loss or a phone call. Floorplan lenders then hold reserves and audit constantly because they cannot see the cash in transit.
solution: When a floored car sells, the dealer requests a bridge with the payoff quote, bill of sale and contract or funding-approval docs (LLM-parsed). We verify the sale with the listing signal (retail-sale signature) and cross-check the payoff quote, then wire the payoff directly to the floorplan lender, so cash never touches the dealer and cannot be diverted. We are repaid when the retail lender funds the contract, through a lockbox or deposit-account control agreement, or a notice of assignment where the retail lender allows it. The risk is receivable dilution (an unwound or charged-back contract from a creditworthy obligor), not dealer fraud. Underwriting uses obligor identity, the dealer's payoff-lag history, the dealer's unwind and chargeback record, and the listing check. Rollout runs in three phases. (1) A free dealer-side 'Unpaid VIN clock' built on the radar signal is the top of funnel and lets aged sold-not-paid VINs self-select. (2) A capped concierge bridge of up to $25k per unit. (3) Floorplan lenders name Day-Zero as an approved payoff method, in return for lower reserves and audit frequency, and receivables are sold forward to credit funds so the startup stays capital-light.
why_now: Inventory near 88 days' supply and floorplan at SOFR plus 200 to 400 bps tighten dealer cash. Contracts in transit stretch a week or more. After Sky Auto Mall, lenders have less tolerance for late payoffs. Private credit is searching for short-duration, self-liquidating receivables at high gross yield. LLM document parsing plus listing signals make per-deal verification cheap enough to underwrite $150 fee deals, which was not economical with a human ops desk.
revenue_model: A fee of about 0.5 to 0.7 percent of the payoff per roughly 9-day bridge, which is about 25 percent annualized gross, plus a 10 to 20 percent referral share to the floorplan lender, capital from a credit fund at about SOFR plus 6, and the startup keeping servicing fees and a first-loss or excess-spread slice. Illustration (assumptions): a dealer bridging 15 deals a month at $22k averages about $100k outstanding and pays about $2.1k a month. 5,000 dealers at that size is roughly $500M outstanding, about $125M of gross yield and perhaps $50M to $60M net after capital cost and losses. A $99 to $199 per dealer per month clock subscription is the top-of-funnel product.
non_obvious_insight: The listing-disappearance signal is too noisy to accuse a dealer but precise enough to underwrite a nine-day secured advance, because a false positive costs a declined bridge and not a false fraud allegation. Paying the floorplan lender directly makes the lender's SOT exposure structurally zero for bridged deals, so the lender is a willing distributor and co-subsidizer, and no lender integration is needed at the start because the dealer supplies the payoff quote. Detection was always a workaround for a timing mismatch that capital can simply remove.
first_30_days: Ask two independent floorplan lenders to name their 10 dealers with the most aged, late payoffs for timing reasons and to introduce us. Draft a term sheet with one credit fund or family office for a $500k to $1M pilot facility. Engage commercial-finance counsel on state licensing (some states license commercial lending and receivables purchases). Build the dealer-side Unpaid VIN clock as a landing page plus a manual crawler for the pilot dealers' sites. Aim to sign LOIs with 5 dealers and one capital source, and run the first three concierge bridges by hand to measure dilution, decline and cycle time.
lineage: mutation of I0218 ('Sold-Out-of-Trust Radar for Floorplan Lenders'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: In-house 'website VIN vs floorplan VIN' comparison (SAS Global Forum paper, 'PROC HTTP: Using the Web to Combat Fraud in Auto Finance During a Global Pandemic'), Vero Technologies (VeroOS), SBS Digital Audit (SBS Software), LotCount. White space: Among the products I could find, none sells the specific signal in this idea: an external-behavior signal (a floored VIN vanishing from the dealer site or marketplaces) checked against the lender's own payoff ledger on a running clock, with a ranked daily queue. Existing offerings cover other things. Physical or photo audits (CSI, LotCount, SBS Digital Audit, Netresult) are periodic and dealer-cooperative. Platforms (Vero, Solifi, Alfa, SBS servicing) analyze the lender's own payment and title data. Bank-data tools (Plaid-style) watch dealer cash. DRN covers location. The unserved wedge is mid-size and small lenders that lack data-science teams: independent floorplan companies, credit unions and community banks with dealer lines, and third-party audit firms that need risk-based audit targeting. It is strongest for used-car and buy-here-pay-here dealers, where captives' retail-delivery reports do not exist. Caveats that shrink the white space: (1) captives see retail deliveries within days and can build the signal in-house, and the SAS paper suggests at least one lender did; (2) Vero, SBS and Cox/NextGear could bolt on the signal; (3) a listing that disappears is a noisy signal (wholesaled, transferred, in recon, or the dealer never lists), so precision must be proven; (4) marketplace scraping has terms-of-service risk, so a licensed feed such as MarketCheck is likely needed. | How this version avoids them: None of the parent's competitors puts capital at risk or takes payoff timing risk. Vero, Solifi, SBS, LotCount, CSI, Netresult, DRN and MOBI all police or monitor, and sell to lenders. This sells to dealers, pays lenders and shares economics with them, so it is complementary and creates no channel conflict. Audit vendors and platforms gain lower-loss books, and if lenders accept Day-Zero they need fewer audits, which is a threat to audit revenue but a benefit to lenders. NextGear and Cox is the real latent competitor because it owns floorplan plus Dealertrack contract flow, but it can serve only NextGear dealers, while independents will not send their dealers to a Cox product. The parent's research did not cover contract-in-transit funding or dealer factoring providers, so checking those incumbents is step zero. Regulatory and capital risks are the main reasons this is the highest-variance offspring.

title: Shared-Aide Pods for 55+ Apartment Buildings
one_liner: One on-site aide team serves 6-10 residents in the same building, delivering assisted-living-style help at a fraction of 1:1 home-care cost.
customer: Owners and operators of independent-living and 55+ apartment buildings (market-rate, senior LIHTC and HUD-202 properties). The payers are middle-income residents and their families, who can't afford $75-130k a year and are stuck on waitlists.
problem: Home care is sold as one aide per client per hour ($35 an hour, about $80k a year for 44 hours a week) only because of legacy billing. Assisted living is at 90% occupancy with almost no new supply before 2030. Residents who age past independent living either move out or go without.
solution: A licensed home-care agency subsidiary (or partnership with one) posts 2-3 aides per shift inside the building. They run scheduled 15-45 minute ADL, medication-reminder, meal-setup and toileting visits, plus overnight response. Dispatch software handles acuity tiers and in-building routing (floors, elevators). Residents buy monthly tiers of about $1,800-3,500, and the property gets a retention amenity.
why_now: NIC MAP shows 57 of 99 metros above 90% occupancy, units under construction at a 2012 low, and no meaningful new supply before 2030. Medicaid HCBS is walled off by 15-month waitlists and labor is scarcer after the 2026 visa pause, so stretching each aide across more clients is the only lever left.
revenue_model: Monthly resident subscription by care tier, with a revenue share or amenity fee to the property owner. Later, Medicaid HCBS or managed-care billing for pods in affordable senior buildings.
non_obvious_insight: Aide hours are cheap to make dense (no drive time, no client-hour minimums) but are priced as if they were mobile. The gap between 1:1 pricing and 1:8 cost is the whole business, and only a property-anchored operator can capture it. Assisted-living-without-the-license is a real category nobody has scaled.
first_30_days: Sign a 90-day pilot with one 100-200 unit 55+ property in a tight market. Subcontract to an existing licensed agency to move quickly, staff a two-aide pod, and target 15 residents at about $2,200 a month. Track aide minutes per resident and move-out avoidance.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: National Church Residences (NCR), SASH (Support and Services at Home, Vermont), Selfhelp Community Services (SHASAM), PACE programs (National PACE Association) and PACE-plus-housing projects. White space: Caveat on process: the session's WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200) before I could run any search. I researched only by fetching about 20 known URLs directly and by using prior knowledge. "No scaled startup found" therefore means not found, not verified absent. Rerun 6-8 searches (Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, 'shared aide' and 'cluster care' startup terms) before committing capital.

What looks unserved: (1) A private-pay, tiered, per-building shared-aide subscription in market-rate or workforce 55+ apartment buildings that are not part of a campus. Existing players are either nonprofit coordinator programs (SASH, Selfhelp, NCR), Medicaid or state-licensed programs (PACE, NJ-style ALP), or campus operators (Brookdale). I found no venture-scale company selling this. (2) A dispatch and acuity-tiering software layer for in-building routing (floors, elevators, overnight response). Nothing I fetched showed one.

Serious risks that shrink the white space:
- Licensing. Under Minnesota 144G.08, sleeping accommodations plus any 'assisted living services' (personal care, toileting help, medication reminders, meal setup, safety checks) under contract requires an assisted-living license. Subsidized housing is excluded unless marketed as assisted living, and the statute does not address a property owner that arranges a home-care provider on site. 'Assisted-living-without-the-license' is therefore legally fragile in many states, especially with an owner revenue share and overnight response, which look like 'holding out'.
- Unit economics. Two aides per shift is 17,520 aide-hours a year, about $400-500k loaded at roughly $23-28 an hour. Spread over 15 residents at $2,200 a month ($396k a year) that is break-even at best. At 6-10 residents the cost per resident is about $4,000-5,000 a month, which is above the stated $1,800-3,500 tiers. The idea's own numbers are internally inconsistent (6-10 residents in the one-liner, 15 in the pilot).
- Substitutes. BAYADA and franchise agencies already market to senior-living partners, and NCR and Brookdale could add pods in-house.

title: Payoff-Triggered Refund Recovery for Credit Unions
one_liner: A payoff-desk plug-in that finds the unearned GAP and service-contract refunds the moment a member pays off, and applies unearned add-on credits in repossession deficiencies. It goes through lenders, not SEO, so it reaches the borrowers the consumer refund sites can't.
customer: Credit unions and regional auto lenders (payoff and collections departments). The lender pays a small SaaS fee or takes a share of recovered money. Second wedge: consumer bankruptcy and debt-defense attorneys and legal aid, at $99 per deficiency audit.
problem: When a borrower pays off early, trades in, or has the car totaled or repossessed, they are owed the unearned pro-rata part of GAP, service contracts and other financed add-ons. Refunds are not automatic. Not the dealer, not the lender and not the administrator processes them, and consumer-refund sites exist because so few people claim. The incentives point the wrong way. The dealer suffers a commission chargeback, so it stalls. The administrator profits from non-cancellation. The lender never owned the product. The borrower doesn't know. In repossession, unearned add-on credits should reduce the deficiency the borrower is sued for, and they rarely appear on deficiency notices. Roughly 3M repossessions a year and subprime 60+ day delinquency at a 32-year record of 6.9% in January 2026 make this a very large pool of missed money.
solution: Ingest the closed-loan document image or loan tape, read the itemized products and financed amounts from the retail installment contract, and match each to its administrator. Compute the pro-rata or earned-basis refund by state rule (New Jersey, for example, requires an automatic refund within 60 days). Auto-generate the cancellation packet with the lender's payoff letter, odometer statement, signature or letter of authority, and the state statute citation, then track it to payment. Stalled cases escalate to the state insurance department with a complaint file. The moat is a database of roughly 60 administrators' actual cancellation requirements and response behavior, plus the 50-state rule set. The repossession product reconciles deficiency notices against the same data and outputs an attorney-ready exhibit.
why_now: Record delinquencies and about 3M repossessions a year, roughly 84-month loans with about 30% of trade-ins underwater, and long terms mean most loans die early and carry stacked add-ons. Credit unions are under member-experience and fee-optics pressure, and California's SB 766 now requires dealers to keep refund and cancellation records. LLMs can finally read messy contract images and cancellation forms cheaply enough to run at scale.
revenue_model: Credit union pays $3 to $6 per payoff processed, or 20 to 30% of recovered money with no upfront fee. Attorneys pay $99 per deficiency audit or a $499 per month subscription. Later, sell aggregated administrator refund-speed benchmarks to dealer groups and regulators.
non_obvious_insight: The consumer refund sites that exist all have the same weakness: they wait for the borrower to show up. The one moment every party knows the loan ended is the payoff, and the lender's payoff desk is the only place that sees all of them. The refund itself comes from the administrator's pool, and the dealer's chargeback is a fight between the dealer and the administrator. The borrower's claim doesn't depend on the dealer cooperating, so the dealer stalling does not need to hold up the refund.
first_30_days: Build the administrator playbook for the 20 largest GAP and service-contract administrators and the 10 highest-population states. Offer 3 credit unions a free retrospective audit of 500 payoffs from the last 12 months and show them the dollar total of unclaimed refunds. Take a 30% success fee on live recoveries. Simultaneously give 5 consumer bankruptcy attorneys the repossession deficiency audit free on their next 3 cases in return for case studies.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Origence (formerly CU Direct) - loan origination/indirect platform (CUDL), Assurant (F&I administrator and TPA), Unverified: consumer GAP/VSC refund-claim services (contingency), Unverified: in-house lender recovery and collections teams and BPO vendors. White space: Verification was limited. The WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was exhausted before I could run any queries, and only about 15 direct URL fetches were possible, many of which 404'd or were blocked. That leaves three points.

1. I found no direct competitor selling a payoff-triggered GAP/VSC refund plug-in to credit unions. Origence, the dominant CU indirect-lending platform, and Assurant, a major administrator, show no such product on their homepages.

2. Genuinely unserved and specific, if the market read holds:
   - A per-payoff, lender-integrated refund workflow for dealer-sold, financed add-ons at credit unions.
   - A 50-state pro-rata rules engine combined with an administrator-by-administrator cancellation-requirements database.
   - An attorney-ready audit of repossession deficiency notices that reconciles unearned add-on credits. Consumer-bankruptcy and debt-defense attorneys and legal aid are plausible buyers, because the lender's or dealer's incentive runs against the borrower.

3. Weaknesses in the idea as written, from reasoning rather than found evidence:
   - The claim that the lender never owned the product is shaky. Under many state retail installment sales acts, and under the FTC Holder Rule, the assignee or holder can carry refund and credit obligations. That helps demand, as a compliance and UDAAP driver, but it changes the pitch from 'find hidden money' to 'reduce liability'.
   - A 20-30% success fee taken from a member's own refund has poor fee optics for a credit union. It also conflicts with the idea's own member-experience rationale.
   - On payoff, the refund goes to the borrower, so the CU gets no direct economic benefit. The CU's incentive is goodwill and compliance, not revenue.
   - CU vendor due diligence and core/LOS integration will make the sales cycle slow.
   - The California SB 766 citation in the idea did not check out. The leginfo summary I fetched for the 2023-24 bill described an unrelated social-worker licensing bill. Do not rely on that cite until it is confirmed.

title: Independent Herd Audits for Loan Participation Buyers
one_liner: Charge the correspondent banks, credit unions and credit funds that buy pieces of cattle loans they cannot see, using sampling audits and a verified collateral tape sold through bankers' banks.
customer: The participation desk or chief credit officer at correspondent ag banks, credit unions and ag-focused credit funds that buy participations in cattle loans from community banks. Community banks hit legal lending limits and sell off big pieces of $2M+ herd loans. Channel partners are the bankers' banks that broker those participations. Later buyers are pool purchasers such as Farmer Mac-style secondary-market programs.
problem: A participant that owns 80-90% of a cattle loan has never seen the cattle. It relies on the lead bank's annual inspection, and the lead bank has already sold most of the risk, keeps servicing fees and has reason to want the loan to look clean. Participation agreements normally give buyers information and inspection rights, but the rights go unused because sending an inspector to a ranch two states away costs $1,500+ and buyers do not know how to audit a herd. The parent's fraud case (about $2.8M against 850 head, claimed and unverified) sits in the loan size that small banks typically participate out. That is a hypothesis to confirm.
solution: A 'Participation Audit' program sold to the buyer of risk, not the originator. Tier 1 desk audit ($300-500): a document reconciliation (sale-barn and brand records, tag and vet purchases) plus a lien search, compared against the lead bank's inspection report. Tier 2 ($1,200-2,000): adds a vet-attested chute-side scan or a credentialed field inspector, with geotagged photos and an EID or visual tag scan, timed to preg-check, weaning or a scheduled sale. Tier 3: surprise audit triggered by a lead-bank downgrade, a delinquency or a cattle-price drop. Buyers audit a random 15-25% of each pool every year, so every borrower knows the draw could land on them, which deters fraud. Buyers also get a verified collateral tape with loan-level fields (head, class, pregnancy rate, variance, lien position, date). That tape lets them price participations and lets funds bid for them. Bankers' banks embed the service in their participation platform for a 20-25% revenue share.
why_now: Herd rebuilding is debt-financed, so more cattle loans are being participated, and delinquencies are rising. A cattle-fraud headline (claimed in the parent, unverified) makes participants ask why they trust the lead bank's word. Examiner guidance generally expects participants to do their own credit analysis rather than lean on the lead, which is worth confirming with counsel. Non-bank capital has been moving into ag credit and needs diligence infrastructure. Remote document reconciliation makes a $400 Tier 1 audit profitable, where a field-only inspector could never be. Farm-loan stress typically creates an appetite for independent verification.
revenue_model: Per-audit fees: Tier 1 at about $400 and Tier 2 at about $1,500. Add $250/loan/year of monitoring, plus a 20-25% share to the bankers' bank. Data subscription for the verified collateral tape at $2-5K/month per buyer. Later, a 5-10 bps diligence fee on pool trades. Example: a correspondent buyer holding $150M across 150 cattle loans pays 150 x $400 + 38 Tier 2 audits x $1,500 + 150 x $250 = about $155K/yr. Ten such buyers is roughly $1.5M in recurring revenue. Field inspection labor is variable, using vet and tech partners paid per visit.
non_obvious_insight: In a participation, the party with the most money at risk has the least information and holds a contractual right that nobody uses because exercising it is operationally impossible. The buyer's question is not 'is the borrower honest' but 'is my lead bank's report honest'. Independence from the lead bank is therefore the product, and adverse selection disappears because the buyer picks the sample after buying, and randomness is the deterrent. Vets are optional at Tier 2, so vet reluctance no longer blocks the business.
first_30_days: Call 15 people: 5 bankers' banks and correspondent participation desks, 5 community-bank lead lenders that sell cattle participations, and 5 credit unions that buy them. Ask for the inspection clause in an actual participation agreement, whether anyone has ever inspected a participated cattle loan, who did it and what it cost. Find one buyer willing to pay $1,000 each for 5 participated cattle loans and invoke its inspection rights with the lead bank. Time the visits to fall preg-check or weaning days with two partner vets or field inspectors. Deliver five Tier 2 reports and a one-page comparison of what we found against the lead bank's file. Use that comparison to pitch a bankers' bank on adding the program to its participation platform.
lineage: mutation of I0338 ('Chute-Side Cow Counts for Ag Lenders'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global / Where Food Comes From (Beef Passport), Merck Animal Health (Allflex tags/readers, Vence). White space: Caveat first: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already spent when I started, so I ran zero searches. I did direct fetches of about 15 vendor and agency pages, plus GitHub repo searches. Nothing here rules out a direct competitor. The biggest gap is that I could not identify the third-party collateral-inspection firms that lenders already pay for cattle counts, or any startup selling vet-verified herd inventory to lenders. Do not treat 'gap' as 'open'.

What the direct fetches showed: none of the herd-software, EID, tracking or verification vendors I checked advertise a lender-facing 'independent count' product. The vendors were CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global/WFCF, Ceres Tag, Halter, HerdDogg and Gallagher. Merck/Vence returned 403, so I could not check it. Every one of them is a producer-side management or supply-chain tool. GitHub searches turned up no open-source lender-verification tool, only hobby herd apps.

The unserved wedge is a lender-mandated, third-party-attested herd inventory built as a covenant workflow. It would cover the vet-signed chute-side count, a portfolio dashboard, and year-over-year anomaly flags such as head count down, pregnancy rate down, or tags missing versus last year.

Structural weaknesses to be skeptical of:
- Adverse selection: 'borrower-initiated' verification means fraudulent borrowers never opt in. The product only works if lenders make it a loan condition.
- Coverage: a preg-check only counts animals brought to the chute that day, not cattle on other leases or sold or double-pledged since. It does not prove ownership or lien priority.
- Vet liability and willingness: vets may refuse to sign anything that reads as a collateral audit.
- Economics: $2-3/head split 50/50 leaves the vet about $1-1.50/head on top of a preg-check fee that is already several dollars.
- Entry by an existing vendor: IMI Global (WFCF) or Merck/Allflex could add this as a feature. | How this version avoids them: None of the eight researched vendors (CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global/Beef Passport, Merck/Allflex/Vence, Ceres Tag, Halter, HerdDogg, Gallagher) sells to the buyer of risk, and none can, because their paying customer is the producer being audited. IMI verifies claims for marketing programs. Our payer, our channel (bankers' banks) and our product (sample audits plus a collateral tape) differ from the parent's per-head, borrower-facing, vet-split model. The competitors to test are traditional collateral-inspection and accounting firms doing agreed-upon-procedures work. They lack cattle-specific tooling and cannot reach a $400 price point without remote reconciliation.

title: Implant Payment Index for ASC Networks
one_liner: Pool invoice-versus-payment data across physician-owned ASC networks to build the payer-by-procedure benchmark that only payers hold today, and turn it into the reference price index that carve-out contracts cite instead of each ASC's own invoice.
customer: First buyers are ASC management companies, physician-owned ASC networks of 5-40 centers, and state ASC associations, all facing payer contract renewals. Later buyers are ASC developers, lenders and PE sponsors building pro formas, and eventually payers licensing the index.
problem: Every carve-out claim hands the payer the vendor invoice, so payers hold the largest SKU-level implant price database in the country and use it in contract talks. Becker's July 2026 reported that this year's payer talks came down to fine print, implant costs and case-level cost data. ASCs' invoices are trapped in AP, so each ASC negotiates knowing only its own numbers. Drugs have a public ASP benchmark, while devices have none, so carve-outs reference each ASC's invoice. Payers distrust that (invoice inflation, related-party distributors) and demand attachments, which creates the paperwork and the leak in the parent idea.
solution: Wedge product: the Payer Implant Scorecard. From de-identified 835s, case lists and a sample of invoices, per payer and CPT it reports the share of implant lines paid $0, realized payment as a ratio of invoice cost, markup actually realized versus the clause, and how the network's terms compare with peer networks. It ends in a negotiation memo with the dollar impact of each ask. Data is contributed give-to-get, and contributors also get a free carve-out lookback that feeds the recovery business. Governance: cells need at least 5 contributors, data lags at least 90 days, nothing is forward-looking, and outputs are ratios rather than vendor prices, with antitrust counsel reviewing the protocol. Then a quarterly published Implant Reference Index and a Model Carve-Out Clause (index plus X%, no per-claim invoice attachment). Later modules include developer and lender pro formas by payer mix and, eventually, a payer license.
why_now: Implant cost is the central ASC economics story of 2026 (Becker's, March and July 2026). Volume is moving to ASCs as CMS's CY2026 rule reportedly expands the ASC covered list; verify the exact list. Payers are using AI payment-integrity tools that will only get stricter on attachments, which gives them a reason to want an index. Invoice and contract extraction is cheap enough to build the dataset without armies of coders.
revenue_model: Networks pay $25-60k a year, or about $2-4k a facility a month, for the scorecard and quarterly refresh, plus a success fee of 10% of the first 24 months of measured implant reimbursement uplift after a renegotiation, measured on the same 835s. Data and pro forma licenses to developers, lenders and sponsors are later. A payer index license comes only once the index is a contract reference. Bottom-up: about 1,000-1,200 implant-heavy physician-owned ASCs at roughly $30k a year is $30-36M before the index and lender products.
non_obvious_insight: The information asymmetry runs in the opposite direction from what ASCs assume. Payers already hold the invoices, since ASCs have been sending them for years, but ASCs do not hold each other's. Because the deliverable is a ratio (paid divided by invoice cost) and not a price, it can be shared without breaching vendor price-confidentiality clauses. Once contracts reference the index, both sides drop the per-claim attachment process that causes the leak. A neutral index is also something an ASC-billing company or PM vendor cannot publish, since it would expose their own clients' leaks and their customers' data-sharing limits.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 ASC networks or MSOs plus one state ASC association, preferring those with payer renewals in the next 6 months. Week 1: offer a free 'zero-pay scan' that needs only 835s and a case list, showing the share of implant lines (L8699, 027x, C-codes) paid $0 by payer and CPT. Week 2: engage antitrust and health-privacy counsel to sign off on the data protocol and BAA/de-identification. Week 3: for the first network, add 20-30 invoices per top payer and CPT to convert zero-pay rates into dollars. Week 4: deliver the first Scorecard and negotiation memo for a live renewal, and sell a paid $15-25k pilot to two more networks. Kill signal: no network will pool data even under the protocol, or scan results show payers already pay implants at cost-plus almost everywhere.

title: Fees-in-Kind: Harvest Becomes School Fee Credit
one_liner: A weigh-in and ledger service that lets parents pay school fees with maize, beans and potatoes at a transparent price, while schools get cheaper, steadier food supply.
customer: Boards of management, principals and bursars of public boarding and day secondary schools, including the new senior-school cohorts, plus rural private schools. The end users are smallholder parents in maize, bean and potato zones.
problem: Farm households are asset-rich and cash-poor exactly when fees fall due in January, May and August. Schools already accept 'a tin of maize' informally, but the value is whatever the storekeeper or bursar decides, with no receipts. Meanwhile the same schools buy food through brokers at inflated tender prices, and government capitation often arrives late. Children still get sent home over arrears even when the parents' store is full of grain. Food is often the largest line in a boarding school's budget.
solution: A Fee Credit Ledger. Farmers deliver graded produce to the school store or a village collection point. A standard weigh ticket (photo of the scale plus a moisture reading) generates an SMS receipt, and the value is credited to the learner's fee account at a published reference price such as NCPB or the county market average, minus a small handling margin. The school gets a weekly reconciliation. On the buying side, the platform, registered as an AGPO-eligible youth or women group (check how each school's procurement committee applies the 30% reservation), bids for school food supply and sources from the same parents. It pools, grades and quality-checks (moisture, aflatoxin spot test). An add-on is hermetic storage bags on credit so parents can deliver later in the term rather than dumping at harvest.
why_now: The first CBC cohort entered senior school in January 2026, expanding boarding and food demand, and the next cohort arrives in January 2027, so schools are planning Term 1 supply now. Capitation delays keep squeezing school food budgets. Cheap Bluetooth scales, moisture meters and M-Pesa and SMS receipts make a trustworthy weigh ticket trivial. Principals in Kenya talk in tight associations, so one working pilot spreads fast.
revenue_model: A 4-8% handling margin on food flow: schools pay below their current broker-inclusive price and farmers receive above the broker price. Later a per-learner per-term ledger fee (about KES 50-100). Once the ledger produces credit-quality data, short-term financing of fee arrears or school receivables.
non_obvious_insight: In every rural ward the school is the largest, most predictable institutional food buyer, and the 'fee arrears list' is a timing and valuation mismatch, not poverty. Fintechs treat barter as embarrassing or informal, but for smallholders paying in maize is the default. What is missing is fair valuation and a ledger everyone trusts. The AGPO set-aside is an under-used entry ticket for farmer groups into school tenders.
first_30_days: Sign 2-3 principals through your own old high school or a heads' association branch meeting for a one-term pilot in January 2027. Buy two Bluetooth hanging scales and moisture meters (a few hundred dollars), run the ledger on Google Sheets plus Africa's Talking SMS, and recruit 100 parent households at PTA meetings. Set the price at the midpoint between the farmgate broker price and the school tender price. Register the entity for AGPO and open a supplier profile with the school.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Maziwa ni School Fees (Uasin Gishu County + Space AI + Tuiyo Farmers Cooperative), Food4Education (Tap2Eat), Zeraki (Zeraki Finance), SchoolPay (Uganda, Kenya, Zambia). White space: Nobody I found offers a grain, bean or potato fee-credit ledger for schools. Google News, site fetches and GitHub search turned up no startup, cooperative product or open-source tool that gives standard weigh tickets, SMS receipts and a published reference price. The practice is real but informal, and it is ripe for a trust layer.

Unserved specifics:
(1) Secondary boarding and senior schools in maize, bean and potato zones. Uasin Gishu has taken dairy, and Food4Education owns primary school meals.
(2) Fair valuation and receipts for staples. Principal Kegoro at Nyabisia Secondary (Kisii) says 'we accept them to bring maize or beans, then we value them and receipt them', which is exactly the informal, discretionary step to standardise.
(3) A per-school reconciliation of in-kind credit against arrears lists. Zeraki Finance and SchoolPay show no in-kind receipt type.
(4) Linking fee credit to the school's own kitchen demand, so the grain never needs to be sold on.

Risks that shrink the white space:
(a) The supply-side tender and AGPO piece is weak. IDRC reports only 1-2% of AGPO opportunities reach women, youth and disability-owned firms, with 90-day-plus payment delays and kickback demands. Schools buy 65% from brokers by manual tender.
(b) 2026 is a maize shortage year. The deficit is about 5.4M bags, flour is at KES 153-163 per 2kg, and 53% of smallholders cite lack of surplus. Farmers may hold grain back, and valuation disputes will be sharp.
(c) Tickets for day schools are small. The proposed day-school fee is KES 7,675, against KES 53k-88k for boarding.
(d) One entity being fee-credit collector and tender supplier to the same school invites a conflict-of-interest problem.
(e) Storekeepers and brokers benefit from the current opacity.
(f) Absence from news is not proof of absence. WebSearch was exhausted and Crunchbase and Product Hunt were blocked, so a stealth or very small pilot cannot be ruled out.

title: Vet-Verified Herd Exposure and Outbreak Index
one_liner: Rural large-animal vets sell two things from one app: borrower-approved, chute-side verified herd counts for ag lenders, and anonymized weekly syndrome tallies whose denominators come from those counts, giving lenders, insurers and traders a true disease-rate signal.
customer: Community banks and Farm Credit lenders (verified herd reports), livestock insurers and reinsurers, cattle analytics desks, packers and feedlot risk managers, animal-health company territory teams, and state animal health boards. Supply side is 25-50 large-animal practices.
problem: Lenders can't verify how many cows exist or where they are, and vets sit on that data unused. Vets can see outbreaks weeks before the state does but their tallies have no denominator, so a count of abortions means nothing without knowing how many bred cows are in that ZIP3. Vets also refuse to police clients, so neither product works if it feels like surveillance.
solution: One vet app and one relationship. At preg-check and weaning, the vet logs every head by EID or tag scan, age class, pregnancy status and location. The borrower approves sharing with a single tap, and the lender gets a timestamped Verified Herd Report. Every week the same vet sends a 30-second SMS tally by syndrome (abortion clusters, maggot wounds, sudden deaths, respiratory, milk drops), aggregated with k-anonymity. Outputs are a per-1,000-head regional index for subscribers, a lender portfolio dashboard with a regional disease overlay, and later an exposure-plus-hazard dataset for livestock insurers.
why_now: Fall preg-check season is live now, so the first verified counts can be collected this quarter. Screwworm and other disease anxiety has traders, insurers and state boards asking for leading indicators. The vet-as-verifier trust position is the same in both products, so one sales conversation with each practice covers both.
revenue_model: $2-3 per head per verification, split about 50/50 with the vet, charged to borrower or lender. $500-2,000 per month lender portfolio dashboards. $2-10k per month institutional subscribers for the outbreak index. $100-300 per month revenue share to each contributing practice on top of the per-head fee. Later, data licensing and pricing support for livestock disease cover.
non_obvious_insight: Verified herd inventory is an exposure layer, and vet syndrome tallies are a hazard layer, which is exactly what an insurer needs to price livestock disease cover. Neither layer alone can be underwritten. The denominator also lets the index read the 'absence of calls' signal properly, since call volume per 10,000 head falling during a quarantine looks different from a quiet region. Two revenue streams turn vets from reluctant borrowers' auditors into advocates: verification is borrower-initiated and tallies are anonymized, so the conflict-of-interest objection goes away.
first_30_days: Sign 3-5 rural practices in TX, OK, KS or NE that each do thousands of head of fall preg-checks, and pitch 3-4 community-bank ag lenders via the state bankers' association ag committee. Run about 10 borrower pilots at $2/head with a form-based app and a PDF report. In parallel, start the plain SMS weekly tally with 25 practices and a free regional newsletter as the give-to-get hook. Backtest screwworm lead time against official confirmation dates and pitch 3 analytics shops for a $1-2k per month paid pilot.
lineage: hybrid of I0338 + I0199 (Chute-Side Cow Counts for Ag Lenders + Rural Vet Call Logs as Outbreak Early Warning). Why stronger: Cow counts alone are a small per-head fee and the outbreak signal alone is a free-data-for-nothing pitch to vets. Combined, vets earn twice from one workflow, the outbreak index gets denominators nobody else has, and the herd data gains a hazard overlay, which opens the much larger livestock insurance and reinsurance buyer that neither product reaches alone.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global / Where Food Comes From (Beef Passport), Merck Animal Health (Allflex tags/readers, Vence). White space: Caveat first: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already spent when I started, so I ran zero searches. I did direct fetches of about 15 vendor and agency pages, plus GitHub repo searches. Nothing here rules out a direct competitor. The biggest gap is that I could not identify the third-party collateral-inspection firms that lenders already pay for cattle counts, or any startup selling vet-verified herd inventory to lenders. Do not treat 'gap' as 'open'.\n\nWhat the direct fetches showed: none of the herd-software, EID, tracking or verification vendors I checked advertise a lender-facing 'independent count' product. The vendors were CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global/WFCF, Ceres Tag, Halter, HerdDogg and Gallagher. Merck/Vence returned 403, so I could not check it. Every one of them is a producer-side management or supply-chain tool. GitHub searches turned up no open-source lender-verification tool, only hobby herd apps.\n\nThe unserved wedge is a lender-mandated, third-party-attested herd inventory built as a covenant workflow. It would cover the vet-signed chute-side count, a portfolio dashboard, and year-over-year anomaly flags such as head count down, pregnancy rate down, or tags missing versus last year.\n\nStructural weaknesses to be skeptical of:\n- Adverse selection: 'borrower-initiated' verification means fraudulent borrowers never opt in. The product only works if lenders make it a loan condition.\n- Coverage: a preg-check only counts animals brought to the chute that day, not cattle on other leases or sold or double-pledged since. It does not prove ownership or lien priority.\n- Vet liability and willingness: vets may refuse to sign anything that reads as a collateral audit.\n- Economics: $2-3/head split 50/50 leaves the vet about $1-1.50/head on top of a preg-check fee that is already several dollars.\n- Entry by an existing vendor: IMI Global (WFCF) or Merck/Allflex could add this as a feature. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SAVSNET / FAVSNET (University of Liverpool), Morrison Swine Health Monitoring Project (Univ. of Minnesota) and Swine Health Information Center (SHIC), Equine Disease Communication Center (US Equestrian), USDA APHIS / NAHLN and Texas Animal Health Commission (mandatory reporting). White space: Verdict basis: I found no commercial or non-commercial system that turns weekly counts from US large-animal (cattle) vet practices into a regional syndromic index sold to institutional buyers. I could not test that claim against Crunchbase, YC, TechCrunch or Product Hunt, so treat it as unconfirmed on the startup side.

What exists today:
- Academic systems, mostly in Europe (SAVSNET/FAVSNET in the UK).
- A 2025 scoping review of 126 animal syndromic systems: 67 percent were still proof-of-concept, only 20 percent were fully operational, and it noted that even established systems are vulnerable to loss of funding. Operational ones were mostly government run. This is a nearby-review finding, not proof that nobody is building this in the US. Source: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&retmode=xml&id=40327964
- Free industry models such as MSHMP (swine) and the equine EDCC.
- Companion-animal practice data businesses (Animalytix, Vetsource).
- Government mandatory reporting, which now covers confirmed and suspected screwworm within 24 hours in Texas.

Unserved, specifically:
1. Pre-confirmation, syndromic, cattle-specific signals: abortion clusters, maggot wounds, sudden deaths and milk drops, at ZIP3 or county level, weekly. Government reporting only covers confirmed or suspected reportable disease.
2. A denominator and absence-of-calls signal that no current system produces.
3. A decision-grade product for private actors who face NWS movement restrictions and have no ground-level feed: sale barns, order buyers, feedlots, packers, insurers and animal health territory teams.

Structural risks that keep this a gap rather than open:
- Government and free alternatives (TAHC and USDA public case counts, EDCC-style free alerts) satisfy much of the need.
- Vets are legally obligated to report suspects to TAHC, so a private feed adds little for confirmed cases.
- Privacy and trade-implication concerns were the top barrier in an Australian stakeholder study (https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&retmode=xml&id=40037116).
- Selling vet-sourced early disease signals to commodity funds carries legal and ethics exposure (material non-public information, duty-to-report conflicts).

title: Section 8 Rent-Increase Deadline Capture Service
one_liner: A tracker that knows each voucher tenant's lease anniversary, sees the new FY2027 payment standard, and files the landlord's rent-increase request inside the tight 60-day window before a year of raise is forfeited.
customer: Small landlords with 1 to 50 Housing Choice Voucher units, especially out-of-state investors in Section 8-heavy markets such as Memphis, Cleveland, St. Louis and Indianapolis. Small PM firms with voucher portfolios are the second segment.
problem: Housing-authority payment standards rose for FY2027, but a new standard does not flow through to an existing tenancy on October 1. It applies only at each tenant's lease anniversary. The owner must send a written request within a typically tight window, often 60 days before that date, or forfeit the increase for a year. Each housing authority has its own forms and dates. Most small owners never map the anniversary dates, so they leave real money uncollected. One market analysis found 3-bedroom increases of 6 to 12%, with a median of 10%.
solution: The landlord uploads photos of their HAP contracts and leases, and the tool extracts tenant anniversary dates and current contract rents. The team maintains a database of housing-authority payment standards and each authority's request process (scraped from PHA PDFs and notices, human-verified). For each unit it computes the increase headroom, alerts at 90, 75 and 60 days before the window closes, and generates the authority-specific rent-increase request letter or form. It tracks proof of submission and logs who was contacted and when. It also flags likely mistakes in the original rent-reasonableness record (wrong bedroom count or square footage) that justify a correction request mid-lease.
why_now: FY2027 standards take effect around October 1, 2026, and today is 2026-09-28. Anniversary windows are opening across the country right now. The forum thread on this appeared within days, and the one-year forfeiture is a hard deadline that makes people spend money.
revenue_model: Success-aligned pricing: $5 per unit per month, plus 1 month of the captured increase for each unit where the request is approved. On a $1,300 rent and a 10% bump, that is $130 per month, or $1,560 a year, per unit. Authority data is the moat; a PM-firm plan can charge per door. Later, a similar deadline tracker can cover annual recertification and inspection dates.
non_obvious_insight: The money is lost to a calendar, not to the tenant or the market, and the people who feel it are the least likely to be organized. A BiggerPockets post titled 'Section 8 rents went up for FY2027. Most landlords won't collect it' says: 'A new payment standard does not flow through to an existing tenancy on October 1'. It adds that owners must submit written requests within a typically tight 60-day window before each anniversary or forfeit the opportunity for an entire year. It reports 3-bedroom rates up 6-12% (median 10%) in nine of ten low-cost ZIP codes, and notes that St. Louis adopted its FY2027 standards effective Jan 1, 2027 (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/52/topics/1301792-section-8-rents-went-up-for-fy2027-most-landlords-wont-collect-it). Out-of-state voucher landlords also struggle with local rules, as in a Cleveland thread on Section 8 inspection standards (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/963/topics/1302305-furnace-and-water-heater-on-wood-platforms-cleveland-section-8-inspection). A separate thread notes Section 8 tenants are 'already at maximum allowable rates' (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/963/topics/1302138-how-realistic-is-it-to-raise-rents-100-on-existing-tenants).
first_30_days: Week 1: hand-build payment-standard tables and request procedures for 3 housing authorities (start with St. Louis, Cleveland and Memphis). Publish a free calculator, 'How much did you leave on the table this year?', in the BiggerPockets Out-of-State and Landlording forums. Weeks 2 to 3: onboard 15 landlords, send requests manually with the templates, and track approvals. Week 4: turn on success-fee billing, and pitch 3 small voucher-heavy PM firms. Target: 15 landlords, 100+ units, and 10 documented approved increases.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: RentsPaid, HAPSecure, TenantKeep, VoucherReady. White space: The reminder and calendar layer is not open. RentsPaid, HAPSecure and TenantKeep already ship anniversary or rent-increase-window alerts at free to $39/mo, and TenantKeep advertises PHA letter generation. A plain tracker with alerts would be a fourth entrant selling against free. All of them are software-only and unfunded. What remains unserved is (1) actually filing the request and chasing it to approval, since TenantKeep says outright that it does not file; (2) a human-verified, authority-by-authority rulebook (window length, form, portal versus mail, comps requirement, tenant signature) in the Section 8-heavy investor markets: Memphis, Cleveland, St. Louis, Indianapolis; VoucherReady explicitly declines to supply PHA numbers; (3) contingency pricing tied to captured increase, when every competitor charges flat SaaS or free; (4) a portfolio leakage audit for small PM firms and out-of-state investors (units at or under the new payment standard with no filed request). Two caveats. Payment standard increases apply to the family's subsidy at the next regular reexam (24 CFR 982.505), not at the lease anniversary, so the pitch conflates two clocks. Rent reasonableness also caps the gain, and BiggerPockets commenters note many voucher units are already at the local maximum.

title: Unit Tests for Benefit Law: Eligibility System Conformance
one_liner: Invert the drill: aim the same synthetic households and adjudicated answer keys at the eligibility software itself, selling H.R.1 conformance test packs to states and system vendors, with an aim to become the standard test suite that state RFPs cite.
customer: State SNAP and Medicaid policy directors and eligibility-system program managers (the people running user-acceptance testing), then the system integrators that build the systems and the AI-tool vendors selling into agencies. First buyers: 2-3 states whose H.R.1 system releases are due between Oct 2026 and Jan 2027 and that already have a UAT process.
problem: The most expensive error is one the system makes identically thousands of times, which no worker training can fix. NC's eligibility system stacked shelter deductions when caseworkers updated rent, and a one-click prompt fixed it and has since been used more than 20,000 times. H.R.1 forces reprogramming everywhere at once (SNAP work-requirement, noncitizen and utility-allowance rules, Medicaid work requirements and six-month renewals due around Jan 2027) under a 75% state admin share and a 6% error cliff. Vendors test their own work. States rarely have independent, boundary-case test data with signed-off expected outcomes.
solution: H.R.1 Conformance Pack v1: about 250 synthetic households aimed at the edges of each changed rule (income at the threshold, mixed-status households, month-boundary changes, shelter and utility interactions), each with an expected outcome and a citation trail to statute, USDA guidance and the state manual. The state's own policy staff sign off the answer key, so we test state policy against state system and do not have to settle federal ambiguity. Where state policy and federal guidance conflict, we flag it as a second deliverable, a QC-risk memo. Delivery fits existing UAT: scenario scripts and machine-readable fixtures with expected results, plus a divergence report. Later: a regression subscription refreshed on every guidance change, vendor pre-certification, and household-level evaluation sets for AI intake and caseworker-assist tools.
why_now: Every state must change its SNAP and Medicaid eligibility logic within months of each other, and Medicaid work requirements and six-month renewals land around Jan 2027. AI tools are entering benefits workflows and agencies have no household-level ground truth to test them against. USDA's FY2025 numbers (41 states above 6%, 10.62% nationally) make a systemic logic bug politically and financially radioactive. Open-source rules engines (PolicyEngine) and LLM-assisted drafting cut the cost of building cases, so adjudication, not authoring, is now the scarce step.
revenue_model: Per-state pack at $40-120k per major rule change, and a regression subscription at $100-250k a year per program per state. Vendor certification runs at $15-50k and AI-tool evaluation runs at $10-30k. Bottom-up: 50 states x 3 programs x about $300k, so $30-60M ARR is a plausible ceiling, and more if state RFPs cite the suite as an acceptance criterion. Much of the spend can draw federal IT matching funds in system-change budgets (verify per program). Prices are unvalidated assumptions.
non_obvious_insight: Independence is the product, in the way UL or a ratings agency is. Vendors cannot credibly grade their own homework, and states cannot staff independent test authorship, so the cornered resource is the adjudicated, state-signed answer key: expert time that compounds across states and rule changes. Testing the machine reaches a bigger error source than training people, and the same answer-key corpus later powers worker drills, QC calibration and AI evaluation. A standard is reachable because states already buy test scripts and would rather cite a neutral suite than write their own.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: pick 12 H.R.1 SNAP provisions from USDA implementation memos and write 60 boundary-case households. Run them through PolicyEngine and through 2-3 states' public online benefit screeners, which needs no system access. Days 10-18: send each state policy director a private divergence report with 3-5 mismatches and an offer of the full pack. Days 15-30: sign 1-2 paid $25-40k UAT-pack pilots with a state policy or IT lead, and start talks with a system integrator's state account team about pre-certification. Recruit 2 ex-state policy and ex-FNS adjudicators to sign keys.
lineage: mutation of I1240 ('Flight simulator drills for county SNAP eligibility workers'), type: 10x-or-inverted

Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Maximus - Accuracy Assistant (SNAP solutions), Code for America - Social Safety Net / SNAP programs, Kognito (sunset) - conversation simulation training, PolicyEngine (open-source US benefit rules engine) and related SNAP repos.
