Maximus's Accuracy Assistant explicitly works 'side-by-side' in live cases and does not train. Code for America and PolicyEngine are systems and rules tools. Kognito-style simulation vendors never targeted eligibility work. (2) Nothing found ties practice performance to documented CQI or corrective-action-plan evidence, which NC's official explicitly asks counties for ('documenting, documenting, documenting'). (3) New-hire ramp-up: Kansas cited turnover and caseworker training complexity as drivers of its errors, and no product measures time-to-competency.

The main threats are structural rather than competitive: (a) the real buyer is the state, which typically owns training (state academies, mandated curricula, training environments in the state eligibility system), and county discretionary budgets may not cover $12k-25k; (b) Maximus or a state's existing LMS vendor could add a practice module; (c) policy variation across states (BBCE, standard utility allowance, county practices) makes per-state case libraries costly to build and keep current; (d) an open-source rules engine (PolicyEngine) lowers the barrier for copycats. | How this version avoids them: Maximus Accuracy Assistant scores live cases for risk and does not test system logic. Code for America and Nava help states build and communicate rules, not produce independent conformance suites. PolicyEngine is the natural supplier and partner (open-source engine, nonprofit, no state-signed answer keys or sales motion), and its SNAP screener validation is not a state-system acceptance test. Vals AI's Public Benefits Bench (with Code for America and the Center for Civic Futures) is a proprietary question-answering benchmark for beneficiary inquiries. It does not test household eligibility or benefit calculations, so we supply the household-level layer and could partner. System vendors and IV&V firms test their own or generic project deliverables, and independence is our counter-position. The Kognito failure is irrelevant here because the buyer is a funded IT/UAT process, not a training budget. State academies are not substitutes.

title: Commissioning Passport: The Data Center Readiness Standard
one_liner: Invert the model: the sponsor pays a neutral party to verify hall readiness once, in a machine-readable ledger every lender, insurer, landlord and offtaker can read, which grows into the standard definition of ready-for-service and the trigger written into loan, lease and backstop documents.
customer: Payers: sub-investment-grade neocloud sponsors and colocation developers, who face 4-6 counterparties each re-diligencing the same hall (issuer-pays). Readers who license access: lenders, DSU insurers, offtakers and backstop providers. Supply side, seeded free: commissioning agents, general contractors and IEs, who become named attestors.
problem: One liquid-cooled hall is diligenced repeatedly. The GPU-loan lender, the landlord's lender, the DSU insurer, the offtaker and any GPU-vendor backstop provider each hire their own advisor or IE, and evidence moves as emailed PDFs. Sponsors lose days on every draw and every counterparty re-asks the same questions. There is no shared definition of 'ready for service'. Lease commencement, financial close and backstop triggers can each key off a different milestone, and a backstop can lapse if construction runs more than about 180 days late. Because credibility is scarce, sponsors post letters of credit or parent guarantees, which is expensive capital to lock up.
solution: Two things. First, an open 'Readiness Ladder' spec, about 40 evidence-backed binary milestones for the last 90 days, published free so it can be adopted like a template. Second, the Passport ledger. Evidence is captured at source (Cx platform exports, utility letters, OEM startup bookings, CDU flush certificates, gear serial and bill-of-lading matches), timestamped and hashed, and tied to a named attestor (Cx agent, IE, OEM technician, utility). We add independent spot audits and a per-party permissioned view. Outputs are a Passport Score, a probability of RFS by date using reference-class priors, and a covenant schedule template (for example 'Ladder milestone L-7 certified in Passport') that counsel can drop into loan, lease and backstop documents so RFS is defined once. First product, sellable within 6 months, is the 'Draw Pack': within 5 business days of a draw or tranche request, we convert the sponsor's own commissioning evidence into a verified Passport snapshot that the lender has agreed to accept. It costs the sponsor $15K per pack or $8K/month per hall. Pilots go to sponsors that lenders cap, for whom verified readiness is a currency. The capture workspace is free for Cx agents and GCs, which seeds the supply side.
why_now: Lenders are capping neocloud exposure, deals are stalling on credit and some operators demand letters of credit or parent backing. Multi-party GPU structures with vendor backstops mean the same hall gets underwritten by many parties at once. The first-principles cost stack changed: turning IST results, punch lists and flush logs into structured pass/fail facts used to take a 3-person review team, and document AI now makes one reviewer per hall economically feasible. That makes portable verify-once evidence cheap enough to sell to the party that would otherwise pay for every counterparty's separate review. It would not have worked in 2019, when there was no GPU-debt market and no extraction tooling.
revenue_model: Issuer-pays verification at $15K per pack or $8-12K/month per hall. Read-side seats for lenders, insurers and offtakers at $40-150K per year, free for the first year to any lender that writes the Ladder into its documents. Licensed Passport Score and delivery-time benchmark indices for funds and reinsurers. Later, lenders offer margin step-downs or lower letter-of-credit haircuts for Passport-verified halls, and we take a fee from the sponsor's saving. Scale illustration: 150 halls under continuous verification at about $100K per year blended is about $15M revenue, with data licensing on top.
non_obvious_insight: Verification is a public good with a payer problem, and the answer is the one project-finance already uses. IEs are borrower-paid but lender-selected, and rating agencies are issuer-paid. The independence safeguards are a lender-vetoable attestor panel, published methodology and an audit trail. For the sponsor the product sells speed and a cheaper substitute for letters of credit and parent guarantees, not virtue. The moat is a cornered dataset: durations by OEM, utility, GC and hall type across every verified hall, which makes forecasts better as more halls join, so the network effect is in the prior. Counter-positioning also works: incumbents bill by the hour for each counterparty, and a portable verify-once artifact cannibalizes that repeat billing. The standard is won by whoever gets its definition of RFS into the legal templates first.
first_30_days: Publish Ladder spec v0.1 and teardowns of 2 publicly delayed projects, built from public documents. Recruit 4 Cx leads and one finance lawyer to draft the covenant schedule. Interview 15 sponsors and 10 lenders to measure which draw-package friction costs the most days and dollars. Sign 2 design partners: one sub-IG neocloud sponsor with a live delayed-draw facility, and its lender, who agrees in writing to accept the pack. Run the service by hand ('Wizard of Oz'): shared drive, spreadsheet and document-AI extraction, with no product build yet. Success by day 45: one lender accepts a Passport pack in place of a second-round advisor visit. Riskiest assumption to test first: sponsors will pay for verification that lenders accept, and lenders will accept sponsor-paid attestation. If not, fall back to Offspring 1 (lender-paid) and keep the ledger as a by-product.
lineage: mutation of I0365 ('Ground-Truth Diligence for GPU-Backed Lenders'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SynMax Vulcan (with Industrial Info Resources data partnership), Currence (formerly Sightline Climate), Epoch AI Frontier Data Centers Hub, SemiAnalysis (consulting, AI Datacenter Model, ClusterMAX). White space: The unserved wedge is narrow but real. (1) No product found in this session combines a binary, evidence-backed 'Readiness Ladder' for the last 90 days before RFS (utility energization letter, MV gear energization, Cx Level 4/5 and IST pass/fail counts, CDU flush and pressure tests, fiber acceptance, punch-list burn-down, OEM startup-tech availability) with a probabilistic RFS-by-date output and draw or covenant triggers. (2) Satellite and database vendors (SynMax, IIR, Currence, Epoch) cover the exterior and the announced schedule, and their materials do not claim commissioning or energization evidence. (3) GPU-deal technical advisors, as described by Peony, focus on fleet, telemetry and power documents rather than data hall commissioning. (4) Traditional IEs are slow, tied to a single lender or borrower, and priced for large project-finance deals. A fixed-fee, two-week, desk-plus-site 'second opinion' for a private credit desk, insurer or offtaker appears unserved. (5) The offtaker and backstop side (AI labs signing take-or-pay capacity, Google or Nvidia-style backstop providers) is structurally underserved because IEs work for lenders. Risks: incumbent IEs and Cx firms can add this as a service line, SemiAnalysis could bolt it on, and the business is people-bound (bench of ex-Cx leads) with limited software moat. Access to sites, contractors and Cx records depends on borrower cooperation, which means lender-imposed information covenants or offtaker leverage. | How this version avoids them: Traditional IEs (Sargent & Lundy markets data center commissioning oversight and lender due diligence, so they are real incumbents): the Passport makes them attestors and partners, so they are a supply-side channel, not a rival. This also blunts the incumbent-adds-a-service-line risk, because their work becomes an input to our ledger. SynMax/IIR, Epoch, Currence: exterior and desk data, taken as inputs and potential co-marketing or referral partners. SemiAnalysis: paid research and ratings-style brands for neocloud operations, not hall-level evidence, and possibly a distribution partner for the index. Peony: a data-room vendor for fleet and telemetry files that could add a Cx module, so it is the closest emerging rival to watch, or an integration partner. Uptime Tier: a one-time end-of-build certificate on design and performance, not a continuous last-90-days schedule ledger. Risks I could not verify: whether lenders will accept issuer-paid evidence, and whether an established engineering firm would launch a competing 'portable' standard once the concept is visible. Publishing the spec early and embedding it in legal templates is the defense.

title: Rural County Night Desk for Hospitals and Jails
one_liner: One pool of licensed remote night nurses and NPs sold as a county bundle: the recorded independent second RN for the critical access hospital, and the video screening that lets a deputy clear an arrestee for booking without a four-hour ER trip.
customer: Chief nursing officers and pharmacy directors at critical access hospitals, county sheriffs and commissioners, state hospital associations, county risk pools, and malpractice and captive insurers, all reached through the same rural-county channels.
problem: At 3am a rural county has three nurses on at the hospital and one or two deputies on the road. The nurse who is supposed to witness a narcotic waste or double-check a high-alert drug is mid-code, and the deputy with an arrestee is stuck in that same ER for hours, leaving the county unpatrolled. Each problem alone is too small to support a dedicated clinical team.
solution: Start with the $150 tablet-and-camera cart at the dispensing cabinet: a remote RN appears within 60 seconds, watches the waste on video, and attests, with a time-stamped clip and an audit log matched to the cabinet record. Add a booking-desk kit (vitals, pulse oximeter, glucometer, breathalyzer) with a physician-signed, ACEP-based clearance protocol and 24/7 RN and NP video screening ('fit for booking with monitoring plan', 'needs ER now', 're-check in 2 hours'). Both run on one recording platform, one compact-licensed clinician pool, one supervising physician and one malpractice policy. The county gets a single dashboard showing diversion-audit coverage, ER visits avoided and 'deputy hours returned to patrol'.
why_now: Rural hospitals are staffed thinly at night and rural jail deaths and diversion are in the news, so both insurers and risk pools are actively looking for evidence-grade controls. Compact licensure and cheap video hardware let a small team run a multi-state night pool for the first time.
revenue_model: $1,500-2,500 per hospital per month plus per-event fees above volume, and $2,000-3,500 per county per month for about 40 jail screens plus $85 per extra screen, so roughly $4-6k per month for a county bundle. Discounts through malpractice insurers and county risk pools convert to distribution. Gross margin of 40-50% at a pool of about 8-12 hospitals per RN per night.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing is the same: a credentialed, recorded, independent clinician on camera at 3am, with a defensible protocol. The evidence infrastructure (timestamped video, audit log, physician-signed protocol) that proves a diversion witness also proves a jail clearance, so one product convinces both insurers. Waste events cluster around medication passes while booking clusters around bar close and weekends, so the two workloads plausibly smooth each other out, and a pilot can confirm that before hiring. The hospital is a natural co-payer, since every cleared arrestee is an ER visit it no longer has to staff for free.
first_30_days: The founder, a rural ER nurse, recruits 6 per-diem or retired RNs with compact licenses plus 1-2 NPs on remote night hours. Write the clearance protocol with a supervising rural-ER physician and have one county attorney review it. Pick one county with both a critical access hospital and a jail the founder knows. Offer the hospital a free 30-day cabinet pilot and the sheriff a $1,500, 60-day booking-desk pilot. Bring the combined numbers (waste attestations logged, ER trips avoided, deputy hours saved) to the state hospital association and the county risk pool.
lineage: hybrid of I0016 + I1025 (Remote Second-RN for Rural Night Shifts + Tele-Clearance for Sheriffs' Booking Desks). Why stronger: Each parent has the same expensive fixed costs (clinician recruiting, compact licenses, recording platform, physician oversight, malpractice) and a small revenue per site. Pooling spreads those costs over two products sold to overlapping counties, lets one relationship close a larger $4-6k per month deal, and lets two insurers see one shared evidence trail, which raises ACV and lowers cost per sale versus either service alone.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: MIDAS Healthcare Solutions (MidasVIEW / Anytime Witness, aka V.I.E.W.), BD Pyxis Med Link Queue & Waste, Avel eCare, VirtuAlly (with Teledigm Health). White space: Nobody I found sells a shared, pooled, live remote-RN witness subscription to critical access hospitals. The specific gaps are:
(1) Live human supply. MidasVIEW replaces the second person with recorded video reviewed later. Pyxis remote witness still needs a colleague on shift. Virtual-nursing vendors cover admissions, discharges, sitters and documentation. Remote pharmacy vendors cover order verification. Nobody provides a licensed second person on demand at 3am.
(2) Transfusion, high-alert and pediatric double-checks. Asynchronous video cannot substitute for a live independent check before administration. Remote IDC is documented as feasible but under-evidenced, and only a few institutions do it (ONS 2024).
(3) Small-hospital fit. MidasVIEW pilots are at tertiary and children's hospitals. Small facilities lag on diversion controls: only 57% of single facilities actively monitor camera footage, and CAHs lack pharmacy staff to review video the next day.
(4) Insurer-linked audit trail. No diversion vendor sells to liability or captive insurers.
The wedge is narrow and time-limited. Avel eCare, VirtuAlly and the telepharmacy vendors could add a witness line quickly, and MidasVIEW could add live witness routing. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: NaphCare (STATCare 24/7 telehealth), Wellpath, Southern Health Partners, Turn Key Health. White space: Caveat first: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before I could run any searches, so this verdict rests on about 14 direct page fetches. That is far short of the 6-12 searches the task called for, and I found no startup-specific evidence either way. I found no vendor whose page shows a tele-clearance product for booking desks, meaning a remote RN/NP screening arrestees before booking with a time-stamped disposition (fit for booking, needs ER now, re-check in 2 hours). Incumbent jail-health vendors (Wellpath, NaphCare, Southern Health Partners) sell on-site staffing or in-custody care. Avel eCare sells 24/7 virtual clinicians to rural ERs and to law enforcement, but only for behavioral crisis. The unserved wedge is a pre-booking, per-county-per-month subscription for jails too small to justify a contracted health vendor, priced against deputy-hours and ER bills. Hospital-run or jail-staff-run tele-clearance programs may already exist locally and I could not check.\n\nTwo structural risks weaken the wedge and need validating early. First, the pitch says the Nurse Licensure Compact makes cross-state night staffing workable, but the NLC covers RNs, not NPs. As far as I know the APRN Compact was not yet operational, so NP staffing likely needs per-state licenses. Second, a remote clinician clearing an intoxicated or injured person on vitals and video alone shifts head-injury and withdrawal liability onto the vendor. That is a malpractice-insurance and clinical-governance problem, and a risk pool may or may not accept it. Revenue is also thin: 12 counties at $2-3.5k a month is roughly $290k-500k a year, with slow county sales cycles.

title: Pharmacy-Side PBM Ledger for Employers
one_liner: Independent pharmacies hold the half of the PBM ledger that employers never see, which is what the PBM actually paid the pharmacy. Pool it to run spread audits for self-insured employers, and give pharmacies a stay-or-leave calculator for their take-it-or-leave-it PBM contracts.
customer: Two sides. First, independent pharmacies, at $99-199 a month for benchmarking and a network-contract modeler. Second, self-funded local employers, school districts, counties and union funds (from 100 to 5,000 lives), plus the benefit consultants and TPAs that serve them, who pay per audit or a share of verified savings.
problem: The employer sees only what it paid the PBM. The PBM sees both sides and hides one. The pharmacy sees what it was paid and what it paid the wholesaler, but has no benchmark and no idea whether the network offer that arrives every Q4 for January 1 is worse than its peers' terms. Everyone negotiates blind. PBMs threaten a pharmacy with losing about a quarter of its business if it declines, and a plan sponsor cannot verify 'pass-through' claims.
solution: Read-only ingestion of the pharmacy's 835 remittance files and invoice costs from its pharmacy management system (PMS). Output 1) per-drug, per-PBM reimbursement benchmarked against NADAC and an anonymized peer pool. 2) A stay-or-leave model of each 2027 network offer built from the pharmacy's own claims mix. 3) With sponsor consent, a claim-level tie-out of the pharmacy-paid amounts against the employer's PBM claims file. That yields a true spread and rebate pass-through gap in dollars per member, delivered as an audit the employer can use to renegotiate or move to a transparent PBM.
why_now: The contract season for January 2027 is happening right now, which gives a hard deadline and a free entry wedge. Employer fiduciaries are under pressure from ERISA suits over PBM costs, state PBM transparency laws and FTC scrutiny. Pharmacy closures (Rite Aid gone, Walgreens closing about 1,200 stores) have given local officials political will. OCR and LLM parsing of messy remit PDFs now makes onboarding a one-day job rather than a consulting project.
revenue_model: Pharmacy subscription of $99-199 a month, or free in exchange for data. Employer audit fees of about $8k-25k per mid-size sponsor, or 10-20% of first-year verified savings. Data licenses to state employee plans, attorneys general, employer coalitions and consultants at a higher tier.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone in the PBM fight holds half a ledger, and only the pharmacy can prove the gap. Thirty pharmacies in one county reconstruct the local school district's and county government's spread at claim level. Independents will hand this data over willingly because it is the first ammunition they have ever had against take-it-or-leave-it contracts.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 pharmacies through the state independent pharmacy association with the pitch 'we will model your 2027 PBM offers free'. Build parsers for the three biggest PBMs' remit formats (the 835 EDI standard helps). Deliver the first stay-or-leave reports. Hire a healthcare attorney to structure data-use terms, since provider-manual confidentiality clauses and HIPAA de-identification are the main risk. Offer one local school district or county a free pilot spread audit and turn the result into a one-page case study.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Truveris (truAudit / truGuard / Marketplace), Capital Rx (Judi Health), AffirmedRx, SmithRx. White space: Caveat on confidence: my WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before I ran any query in this session. The verdict rests on direct fetches of about 20 competitor and source pages plus GitHub searches, not on a broad landscape scan. It is a provisional 'gap', not a confirmed one.

What I did not find: no company that ingests pharmacy-side remits, benchmarks per-drug, per-PBM reimbursement against a peer pool, models Q4 network offers, and ties pharmacy-paid amounts to an employer's PBM claims file. The employer-side audit market is served: Truveris, benefits consultants, and transparent PBMs that market pass-through. Their audits appear to start from what the PBM hands over, and I found no sign they hold the pharmacy-paid half.

The pharmacy-side gap is plausible. PioneerRx, PQS and CPESN pages show no reimbursement-benchmarking or contract-modeling feature. Not verified: pharmacy services administrative organizations (PSAOs such as Cardinal, AmerisourceBergen Elevate, AAP, Health Mart Atlas) and pharmacy management system vendors may already offer contract review or reimbursement reports to members. Confirm this in customer interviews before building, because the PSAOs negotiate PBM contracts and already hold members' remits.

The specific unserved wedge is a claim-level reconciliation between the pharmacy's actual paid amount and the employer's PBM claims file, delivered as a spread and rebate pass-through gap in dollars per member.

Risks that shrink the white space:
- PBM provider-manual confidentiality clauses and possible antitrust or information-exchange concerns when pooling competitors' reimbursement rates.
- Getting employer PBM claims files with sponsor consent.
- Pharmacy remits are not uniformly 835 files.
- The January 2027 contract window is roughly 3 months away and cannot be met by a product built from scratch.

title: Auto Add-On Refund Cascade: Payoff and Return Desk
one_liner: One refund engine for auto add-ons (GAP and service contracts) with two triggers, California's new 3-day return for dealers and the loan payoff for credit unions, sold through the lender who touches both.
customer: California credit unions and regional auto lenders (payoff and indirect-lending departments), who pay for payoff recovery and can introduce their dealer networks. California independent and buy-here-pay-here used-car dealers selling 30-200 cars a month, who pay per return. Later, MGAs and insurers buying return-risk data.
problem: Dealers with no back office must unwind a returned car (lender, add-on administrators, DMV, sales-tax reversal, commissions) inside a very short refund deadline, and fragmented dealers are expensive to reach. Credit unions leave unearned GAP and service-contract refunds unclaimed at payoff because consumer refund sites wait for borrowers to show up. Both jobs depend on knowing what roughly 60 administrators actually require and how fast they pay.
solution: A shared cancellation-cascade engine: administrator playbook and response-time data, a 50-state pro-rata rule set, and generated cancellation packets tracked to payment. Trigger A (dealers): forward the cancellation notice and the desk notifies the lender, submits administrator cancellations, prepares DMV and tax reversals, calculates refund and permitted deductions, and stores the compliance file, at $195-250 per return or a $99 per month standby plan. Trigger B (lenders): free retrospective audit of 500 past payoffs, then $3-6 per payoff or 20-30% of recovered refunds. Pitch the credit union as the channel: 'Your dealers' returns start hitting your payoff desk October 1. We give your dealer network a standby unwind plan, and your members automatic refunds.'
why_now: California's SB 766 takes effect Oct 1, 2026, two days from today, so the first returns arrive within days. No US state has run a mandatory used-car return at this scale. Roughly 3M repossessions a year, 84-month loans and about 30% of trade-ins underwater mean many loans die early with stacked add-ons, and buyers who suddenly cannot afford the payment are the likeliest to return. LLMs can now read messy contract images cheaply.
revenue_model: Per-return fee of $195-250 and $99 per month per-store standby retainer. Credit union payoff fee of $3-6 per payoff or 20-30% of recovered money. Attorney deficiency audits at $99 each. Phase 2: 10-20% of premium as MGA on a $60-120 per used unit return-risk cover. Phase 3: license the cascade workflow to dealer management systems and eContract vendors, and sell administrator refund-speed benchmarks.
non_obvious_insight: These are one business with two triggers. Every California return teaches the desk how each administrator behaves (what they demand, how fast they pay), which makes payoff-refund collections faster and more predictable, and every payoff audit produces the dollar totals that open lender doors. The credit union's indirect dealer network is the only cheap channel to hundreds of small dealers, and the lender is motivated because a dealer's botched unwind becomes the lender's compliance and funding headache. Return and payoff data together also price the return-risk insurance nobody can price today.
first_30_days: Write the cascade checklist for the 20 most common California indirect lenders and 15 administrators. Approach the California Independent Automobile Dealers Association and 10 high-volume independents with the $99 standby plan and a 24-hour turnaround promise. Pitch 3 California credit unions with indirect programs on a free 500-payoff retro audit plus a dealer-network standby offer. Handle the first 20 returns manually with a spreadsheet and e-sign, and log the time and dollar cost of every step.
lineage: hybrid of I0109 + I1151 (Payoff-Triggered Refund Recovery for Credit Unions + Unwind Desk for California's 3-Day Car Return). Why stronger: The lender relationship solves the return desk's distribution problem, and the return desk hands the payoff product a must-have, time-boxed reason to get a meeting. One administrator database serves both, so unit cost falls with volume and collection speed improves. The combined dataset is what makes the return-risk MGA product priceable, which neither parent can reach alone.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Origence (formerly CU Direct) - loan origination/indirect platform (CUDL), Assurant (F&I administrator and TPA), Unverified: consumer GAP/VSC refund-claim services (contingency), Unverified: in-house lender recovery and collections teams and BPO vendors. White space: Verification was limited. The WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was exhausted before I could run any queries, and only about 15 direct URL fetches were possible, many of which 404'd or were blocked. That leaves three points.

1. I found no direct competitor selling a payoff-triggered GAP/VSC refund plug-in to credit unions. Origence, the dominant CU indirect-lending platform, and Assurant, a major administrator, show no such product on their homepages.

2. Genuinely unserved and specific, if the market read holds:
   - A per-payoff, lender-integrated refund workflow for dealer-sold, financed add-ons at credit unions.
   - A 50-state pro-rata rules engine combined with an administrator-by-administrator cancellation-requirements database.
   - An attorney-ready audit of repossession deficiency notices that reconciles unearned add-on credits. Consumer-bankruptcy and debt-defense attorneys and legal aid are plausible buyers, because the lender's or dealer's incentive runs against the borrower.

3. Weaknesses in the idea as written, from reasoning rather than found evidence:
   - The claim that the lender never owned the product is shaky. Under many state retail installment sales acts, and under the FTC Holder Rule, the assignee or holder can carry refund and credit obligations. That helps demand, as a compliance and UDAAP driver, but it changes the pitch from 'find hidden money' to 'reduce liability'.
   - A 20-30% success fee taken from a member's own refund has poor fee optics for a credit union. It also conflicts with the idea's own member-experience rationale.
   - On payoff, the refund goes to the borrower, so the CU gets no direct economic benefit. The CU's incentive is goodwill and compliance, not revenue.
   - CU vendor due diligence and core/LOS integration will make the sales cycle slow.
   - The California SB 766 citation in the idea did not check out. The leginfo summary I fetched for the 2023-24 bill described an unrelated social-worker licensing bill. Do not rely on that cite until it is confirmed. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ComplyAuto (exclusively licensed by CNCDA), CDK Global (DMS), CNCDA (California New Car Dealers Association), DealerCenter (DMS for independent dealers). White space: Research limitation: the WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200), so no searches were run. That means no Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or forum searches, and no search for startups by name. Everything below comes from direct WebFetch of about 30 primary and vendor URLs, with model-generated page summaries. I found NO dedicated 'unwind-as-a-service' for CARS Act cancellations, but I cannot rule out a small startup. Re-run the startup and forum searches before committing.

The idea's premise is weaker than written. Statute text (SB 766, Civ. Code 1784.43, 1784.31(g), 1784.44, as returned by WebFetch and quoted verbatim by the summarizer):
1. The 48-hour duty is only to cancel the contract and refund the buyer. The dealer 'is not responsible for any delays outside the control of the dealer, including delays attributable to the processing of a refund by a bank, credit card company, or other financial institution.' Check payments get a 2-business-day delay. Lender and administrator lag therefore does not create violation exposure. The exposure is the dealer's cash float and its own process failures.
2. The statute lists no duty to cancel service contracts or GAP within 48 hours. The add-on cascade is a business and recovery problem, governed by existing law and contract terms. It is not a statutory deadline.
3. Permitted deductions are formulaic: a restocking fee of 1.5% of price (min $200, max $600), plus $1 per mile over 250 (capped at $150), plus trade-in liens. They are not damage-based. The claim that permitted deductions depend on condition documentation, which justifies the photo and video capture bundle, does not hold up. What does matter is the 400-mile eligibility gate and the trade-in refund rule. If the trade-in is already sold or in title transfer, the refund is the greater of the agreed value, the sale price, or fair market value.
4. Remedies are non-exclusive (1784.22). No explicit private right of action or civil penalty was found. Enforcement runs through DAs, city attorneys and the DMV, plus existing consumer laws.
5. Dealers already run unwinds. California had a 2-day contract cancellation option with a 2-day refund including sales tax (Veh. Code 11713.21), repealed effective Oct 1, 2026. Failed-financing spot-delivery unwinds are also routine (from my background knowledge, not verified here). Buy-here-pay-here lots hold their own paper, so they have no lender cascade at all. The $195 to $250 per-return price competes with a title clerk or F&I manager plus a DMS 'reverse deal' function.

What remains unserved:
(a) Independent, indirect-financed dealers with no back-office bench. Compliance vendors and associations found are aimed at franchised dealers or at pricing, ad and disclosure compliance.
(b) A per-return calculator and checklist: restocking fee, mileage, the trade-in 'greater of three' refund, lender payoff, F&I commission chargeback, and the administrator-by-administrator cancellation basis, with timers and a 2-year compliance file.
(c) Above all, the dealer's economic loss per return. Dealers lost the fee they could charge for the old cancellation option ($75 to $250 or 1%). Restocking is now capped at $200 to $600, against recon, carrying cost and resale loss. Nobody was found pricing or covering that loss.

title: Deficiency-Suit Add-On Credit Audits for Consumer Defense Firms
one_liner: A flat-fee, 24-hour audit that rebuilds a repossession deficiency from the retail installment contract and shows the unearned add-on credits, notice defects and fee errors the lender or debt buyer left out, sold to the consumer-defense lawyers who already have the client and the deadline.
customer: Consumer-defense and debt-defense attorneys and legal aid offices that defend post-repossession deficiency suits. Start in two or three states chosen from docket data in week 1 (candidates: Maryland, Pennsylvania, Ohio, where notice rules and fee-shifting tend to favor borrowers; confirm before committing). Wedge buyer: small consumer-law firms of 1 to 10 lawyers that take flat-fee or fee-shifting cases, plus 3 to 5 legal aid units.
problem: A repossessed borrower is typically sued 6 to 18 months later, often by a debt buyer, on a one-line balance backed by a thin affidavit. The defense lawyer has about 30 days to answer, no numbers person, and a flat fee or grant-funded hours. The deficiency figure usually does not credit the unearned GAP, service-contract and other add-ons that were rolled into the loan, and may carry defective post-sale notices or inflated fees. Rebuilding it by hand takes a paralegal hours, so most defendants default or settle blind. The parent's borrower-side value is real but lacked a buyer with standing, a deadline and a fee-shifting statute. This buyer has all three.
solution: The attorney uploads the complaint, contract image, pre- and post-sale notices and auction bill. Within 24 hours the tool returns a Deficiency Autopsy PDF: (1) a rebuilt ledger from the retail installment contract (amount financed, itemized add-ons, finance charge, payments, fees); (2) unearned add-on credits owed under the contract and state rule, with the administrator's cancellation requirement and a computed pro-rata figure; (3) a notice checklist against UCC Article 9 and the state motor-vehicle finance act (timing, required content, explanation of the deficiency calculation, commercial-reasonableness red flags such as sale price versus wholesale value, and whether a defective notice bars the deficiency in that state); (4) an exposure sheet covering offsets, defenses and potential statutory damages under UCC 9-625(c)(2) as adopted by the state; (5) draft answer paragraphs, counterclaim language and targeted discovery requests aimed at cancellation records. A human analyst reviews every output at first, later only exceptions. Flat fee only, never a share of a fee award, which avoids fee-sharing problems with non-lawyers (Rule 5.4) and keeps this an attorney work tool rather than advice to consumers.
why_now: Subprime 60+ day delinquency hit a 32-year high in January 2026 and roughly 3M repossessions a year feed a deficiency pipeline that debt buyers monetize through suits. 84-month loans and underwater trade-ins make deficiencies large, so a $99 audit is small next to the dollars at stake per case. LLMs now read messy contract scans, auction bills and notices for cents per case, which was not economic in 2022. Federal consumer-finance enforcement has retrenched since 2025 (verify), so what enforcement remains is private and state-level, and it runs through exactly these lawyers.
revenue_model: $99 per audit; $499 per month for up to 8 audits plus template library for small firms; about $2,400 per year site licenses for legal aid; $750 for attorney-directed analyst declarations. Second, higher-value stream: anonymized pattern reports on defect prevalence by lender, debt buyer and collection law firm (for example, the share of one plaintiff's notices that omit add-on credits), sold to class-action firms and state AG staff at $25K to $100K per report. Audit revenue alone is a small wedge (likely single-digit millions a year), so the dataset and pattern reports are the scale path.
non_obvious_insight: Each audit is a product and a labeled data point. Deficiency defects are systematic because one plaintiff's template produces the same omission in every case, and UCC 9-625 statutory damages attach per consumer, so the pattern is worth far more to class counsel than a single case is to a defendant. The parent's flaw, that lender incentives run against the borrower, becomes the moat: lenders and their in-house recovery teams can never sell this because they are the party being audited. The borrower's claim also needs a number and a deadline, not the dealer's or administrator's cooperation.
first_30_days: Week 1: pull about 300 recent deficiency complaints from public dockets in the candidate states (plaintiff, amount, whether the defendant had counsel) to pick two states and list the 10 heaviest filers; have a consumer-law ethics lawyer review the template for unauthorized-practice and fee-sharing risk. Weeks 2 to 3: ask 15 consumer-defense firms and 3 legal aid units (through NACA, NCLC and state consumer-law listservs) for their next 3 deficiency cases free in return for a written outcome; deliver each audit manually in 24 hours using LLM extraction plus an analyst. Week 4: switch to $99, publish an anonymized 'five places deficiency numbers lie' guide, and log the dollar swing on every case. Target: 30 audits delivered, 10 paid, 5 documented cases where the balance moved by more than $1,000.

title: Carve-Out Audit Kit for Challenger ASC Billers
one_liner: A white-label implant carve-out engine for independent ASC billing companies, who use a free lookback on a prospect or new client as their sales weapon and split the recovered dollars with us.
customer: Independent ASC billing and RCM companies with roughly 8-60 ASC clients. These are the long tail behind SIS/Surgical Notes, National Medical Billing Services and Nimble. The buyer is the owner or head of sales. The ASC still pays the fee, but through its biller.
problem: Billers win ASC clients on percentage fee and references, and the new-ASC wave makes that fight harder. They can't afford implant analysts or invoice-parsing tooling for 30 clients. A startup selling direct to ASCs hits a trust wall, because owners won't hand 835s and contracts to an unknown vendor. Billers already hold the BAAs, the ERA feeds and the contract PDFs. Billers also don't buy 'recovery', because it admits past misses. They buy client acquisition and retention.
solution: White-label 'Carve-Out Desk' with three parts. (1) Lookback as an RFP weapon. For a prospect, or a new client in its first 30 days, ingest 12-24 months of 835s, implant log and AP invoices and return a co-branded Carve-Out Leak Report showing dollars by payer and CPT. The new biller can recover the prior biller's misses with no political cost. (2) Recovery ops. We prepare attachment packets and corrected claims and appeals, and the biller submits, or we do so under the biller's credentials. (3) A prospective pre-bill gate, delivered as upload plus a review queue that works with whichever PM system the biller's clients use, checking invoice attached and L8699/027x coded to trigger the carve-out. Each partner audit adds payer-clause entries to a shared clause library.
why_now: New and converting spine and ortho ASCs are choosing billers now, as CMS's CY2026 ASC rule (CMS-1834-FC) reportedly expands the ASC list; verify the exact list. Payer AI payment integrity makes attachment mistakes costly. Invoice parsing now costs cents, so the audit can be run for a prospect who has not yet signed. Becker's coverage in 2026 shows implant cost is the hot ASC topic, so billers have a live sales angle.
revenue_model: Money flow: the payer pays the ASC as usual. The ASC pays the biller 25-30% of recovered carve-out dollars under a 'Carve-Out Assurance' schedule the biller adds to its contract. The biller remits about 50-60% of that to us, so we take roughly 15% of recovered dollars and the biller keeps roughly 10-12% for near-zero labor. On top, $300-600 per facility per month for the pre-bill gate and a $2-4k flat fee per prospect lookback, credited against the rev-share. Illustrative unit economics, to be verified in pilots: a facility recovering $240k in year one yields about $36k to us plus about $6k of platform fees. Twenty partners with an average of 20 implant-heavy clients each is 400 facilities, which supports a $5-10M ARR outcome.
non_obvious_insight: The biller's incentives are the opposite of the ASC's. Incumbents will not audit themselves, but their challengers desperately want a proof-of-value opener. The moment of highest willingness to pay is a biller switch or a new ASC opening, because the prior party's misses can be recovered with no blame. The channel also removes the hardest part of direct sales: data access and trust arrive through an existing BAA chain. Every partner lookback grows the cross-client clause library, and an incumbent biller who refuses the tool becomes exposed to challengers who use it.
first_30_days: Build a list of about 150-200 independent ASC billers from ASCA and state ASC association vendor directories, Becker's ASC sponsor lists and LinkedIn. Pitch 40 owners by phone with one offer: 'Give me one prospect you're pitching, or your newest client, and I'll return a co-branded carve-out leak report in 10 days, free.' Convert 3 pilots with 2 audits each, run by hand with a coder and a spreadsheet plus an LLM for invoices. Success: at least $100k of collectible carve-out dollars found on 2 of 3 audits, and one biller signing the rev-share and the Carve-Out Assurance add-on. Kill signal: billers say they already catch this and the reports show under 2% leakage. In that case pivot to selling direct to in-house-billing ASCs.

title: Evac Cash: Payout When Ordered to Evacuate
one_liner: A few dollars a month buys a $500-$2,500 wire within hours of an official mandatory evacuation order for your address, covering hurricane, wildfire and burn-scar flood orders.
customer: Renters and lower-to-middle-income homeowners in evacuation zones: Gulf and Florida surge zones, Western wildfire-urban-interface neighborhoods, and LA burn-scar areas. Sold to individuals, through employers of hourly staff (hospitals, hotels, nursing homes, grocers), and through credit unions or municipal 'evac funds'.
problem: Evacuating costs $1,000-$3,000 (gas, hotel, lost shifts, pet boarding) and the money is needed before any claim exists. Cost is a common reason people stay, so the people most exposed are least able to leave. Civil-authority and additional-living-expense cover is slow, receipt-based, often conditional on nearby damage, and many renters lack it.
solution: A parametric contract whose trigger is a legal act. If your geocoded address sits inside a polygon under a mandatory evacuation order, or an NWS flash-flood emergency for a burn scar, the platform pays via FedNow/RTP or a push-to-card within hours. Zone data comes from county emergency-management systems (evacuation-zone platforms and state zone maps). Tiers are priced by zone frequency, with one payout per event per address and a simple app that alerts you and shows your zone. Underwritten via a licensed MGA and fronting carrier, first as employer group policies.
why_now: Address-level, machine-readable evacuation zones are now common. FedNow/RTP make hours-not-weeks payouts cheap. The LA fires of January 2025 made burn-scar exposure vivid, and NOAA CPC/IRI's September 2026 outlooks show a greater than 90% chance of a very strong El Niño this winter, which means heavy rain on fresh burn scars and flash-flood/debris-flow evacuation orders. Parametric reinsurance capacity is plentiful and MGAs want small-ticket distribution.
revenue_model: Premium of roughly $3-$15 per month depending on how often each zone is ordered out (about 1.3-1.5x expected payout), or $1-$3 per employee per month on group plans. The company keeps an MGA commission of 15-25%, plus municipal, nonprofit and employer-funded policies for vulnerable residents. Later it can sell zone-frequency data to emergency managers.
non_obvious_insight: The best parametric trigger is a legal act, not a physical measurement. An evacuation order is binary, public, address-specific and timestamped, so basis risk nearly vanishes. Paying people to leave also changes behavior and saves lives, which makes employers and governments willing co-payers, so the product has two buyers instead of one.
first_30_days: Sign a parametric MGA and fronting carrier. Build the polygon match and instant-payout flow on public evacuation-zone data. Pilot a group policy for about 200 hourly workers at one Gulf hospital or hotel employer and one credit union serving a LA burn-scar community. Offer emergency-management agencies a free 'what zone am I in' tool for distribution. Goal: 500 covered addresses before peak rain season.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Arbol, FEMA Individuals and Households Program (Serious Needs / Displacement Assistance), Homeowners and renters ALE / civil-authority coverage (State Farm, Assurant, Lemonade and other carriers), Jumpstart (parametric earthquake, California). I found no product that pays a flat cash amount to an individual within hours because a mandatory evacuation order covers their address. Every adjacent player triggers on something else. Parametric platforms use physical measurements. FEMA and GiveDirectly pay after the event and need an application or a declaration. Homeowners and renters ALE and civil-authority cover is receipt-based. The unserved wedge is the legal-act trigger, paid out as a flat amount before the trip, to renters and hourly workers, funded by someone other than the individual (county or state emergency management, Medicaid and Medicare Advantage plans, landlords or property managers, credit unions, philanthropy). That funder-pays model is the specific space I found nobody in. Main risks: a carrier could add a flat 'evacuation expense' rider to renters policies, and evacuation-zone data is held by vendors and counties, some under licensing terms that were not checked.

title: Owner-Side Ordering: The Royalty Asymmetry Calculator
one_liner: An advice-only LINE tool that tells franchise convenience-store owners how many fresh items to order and when to mark them down, using the owner's own payoff instead of HQ's.
customer: Franchise convenience-store owners in Japan, especially the many multi-store owners (roughly 55,000 stores nationally, all three chains). They pay a monthly fee plus a share of the waste they cut. First targets are Osaka owners reachable through the franchisee union and owner LINE groups.
problem: The royalty is charged on gross profit calculated as if discarded food never existed. At Seven, HQ absorbs only 15% of disposal cost and the owner absorbs 85%. So HQ's ordering AI and the field counselors (OFC) push order quantities toward what maximizes HQ's royalty, not the owner's take-home. Take a rice ball that costs ¥100 and sells at ¥160. With a 60% royalty on the ¥60 gross profit, the owner keeps about ¥24 when it sells and loses about ¥85 when it is binned. HQ makes about ¥36 on a sale and loses about ¥15 on a discard. The owner-optimal stocking level is far lower than HQ's, and no owner has a tool that shows this. Markdowns would close much of the gap, but staff are reluctant to apply stickers and owners fear the OFC's disapproval.
solution: The owner photographs the daily disposal-scan printout and the hourly sales sheet, or forwards a CSV. The tool never touches HQ systems. Each afternoon it returns a per-category order guide such as 'cut salmon onigiri by 4 at the 16:00 delivery, add 2 tempura udon'. It also gives a markdown clock, for example 'sticker at 20:40, deeper cut at 23:10', calculated from the owner's actual royalty tier, disposal share and sell-through curve. A one-page 'why I ordered less' printout gives the owner data to answer the OFC. Phase two adds an owner-side dashboard showing true hourly wage after royalty and self-labor. It also adds a contract-exit and renegotiation calculator, and anonymized peer benchmarks that owners can use collectively.
why_now: Osaka's minimum wage rises to ¥1,231 on 1 October 2026, up ¥54 after ¥63 last year. Labor is the biggest cost, and waste is the last controllable line item. HQ-side AI ordering is now the default, so owners increasingly follow machine suggestions they cannot audit. Chains have grudgingly allowed markdowns since the JFTC's 2009 order against Seven-Eleven Japan for obstructing them, but owners still lack tools to price them properly.
revenue_model: ¥4,900 per store per month, plus 20-25% of documented waste reduction for the first 12 months. If a store saves ¥80-100k a month, the fee is easy to justify. Multi-store owners get a bundle. Later revenue comes from an owner-benchmark subscription and referrals to specialist franchise lawyers and accountants.
non_obvious_insight: Waste is not a shared problem between HQ and owner. The contract makes it the owner's problem alone, while HQ's revenue is almost indifferent to it. The newsvendor critical ratio for the owner is about 22%, versus about 70% for HQ. Every 'AI ordering recommendation' is optimized for the wrong party's payoff. Nobody built the owner's-side calculator because owners fear retaliation and VCs assume HQ systems are neutral.
first_30_days: Use my three stores as the lab. Photograph two weeks of disposal sheets and hourly sales, then back-test the newsvendor plus markdown model against what actually happened. Build a LINE bot with photo OCR and a spreadsheet engine. Recruit 10 owners from union chat groups and Facebook franchisee groups. Run a free 4-week gain-share pilot with a signed baseline for each store. Publish a one-page 'royalty asymmetry' explainer that spreads owner-to-owner. Convert the pilot to paid at week 5.

competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. title: Recorder Rails: County-Funded Clean Index of Instruments
one_liner: AI re-indexing and compliance scans that counties buy from their own records-modernization funds. In return we hold the cleaned, entity-resolved index of every non-deed instrument, which becomes the data layer for assembly alerts and much else.
customer: County recorders and clerks (about 3,100 counties), who pay first, starting with mid-size rural and exurban counties in data-center and energy corridors where economic development offices also want the assembly view. Downstream buyers are the parent's developers, utilities and funds, plus ag lenders and title-adjacent firms.
problem: The parent's product depends on county-by-county recorder access and on document types that are often wrong ('Other', 'Miscellaneous', 'Agreement'). Ingestion is a grind, bulk commercial-use rules vary, and the good data is scattered. Counties have their own pains: aging archives, mandated redaction of sensitive data, covenant-review requests and property-fraud pressure, all with thin staff. They already spend on indexing and digitization from earmarked funds. Nobody owns a clean cross-county index of non-deed instruments.
solution:
1. Sell the county a fixed-price Hidden Instruments Audit. AI reclassifies its mislabeled and 'Other' instruments from the images, corrects grantor and grantee indexing, flags sensitive-data and statutory items such as discriminatory covenants, and gives the county a corrected index and an economic-development view of large instruments.
2. In the agreement, the county gives bulk access to the images and index at cost, and we keep the right to publish the derived classification and entity graph. The underlying records are already public.
3. Publish an open taxonomy for non-deed instruments, in the manner of MISMO for mortgages, so counties and vendors can adopt it.
4. Keep the labeled corpus and the LLC-family graph proprietary and build products on it: Courthouse Tape alerts, the utility site-control check, landowner tools, alt-data licences and collateral-encumbrance alerts for ag lenders.
why_now: LLM vision has collapsed the cost of reading a scanned page, so a re-index that once cost a labor-intensive vendor per-page fees is now cheap. Counties are under fresh mandates to review archives: covenant-removal laws in a number of states, and reportedly some large counties have already run AI covenant scans (verify which). Property-fraud concern is high. FinCEN's exemption of domestic companies from beneficial-ownership reporting makes primary-record entity resolution more valuable. The large-load land rush gives the resulting index an immediate paying use. Rural counties facing data center proposals want visibility into assembly.
revenue_model: County audits at $9k-$40k per county, fitted under small-purchase thresholds and paid from records-modernization or technology funds, then $5k-$20k a year to maintain. Data licences to funds at $50k-$150k a year. Downstream product revenue per the parent: developer or utility seats at $2k-$8k a month and title packets at $750-$2,000. A plausible year-three target is 300 counties at about $25k, or $7.5M, plus $5M-$10M of licences and subscriptions. Gross margin on data products should exceed 70% once ingestion is standardized.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is county cooperation, not the classifier. So invert who pays. Instead of buying access from counties, we get paid by them to solve a problem they already fund, and the by-product is the corpus. A county that gets a corrected index and a free economic-development dashboard has little reason to block a downstream data feed, and other counties will copy the arrangement. This is a cornered resource plus switching costs that build county by county. Incumbents face asymmetry: indexing and digitization vendors earn from labor-based per-page work, so AI re-indexing at a fraction of the price undercuts their own revenue. Title plants index for title, not for cross-county assembly detection.

If that count is low, shift the wedge to easement and transmission detection. Show each recorder the result: 'We found N large instruments mislabeled as Other.' Offer a $9,500 audit to three counties, and separately sell the free 'who is assembling where' memo to 10 site-selection consultants to fund the corpus. Check each state's rules on commercial use of bulk records and on data-sharing agreements, and get county counsel comfortable.

The main structural doubts I could not test are whether developers actually record option memoranda before announcement, and how many counties allow bulk commercial pulls of document images. | How this version avoids them: The parent's competitors are adjacent data sellers: ATTOM, Regrid and Reonomy sell deeds, mortgages and parcels; Enverus, Paces and GridCARE serve a client's own site; Cleanview, DC Byte and Heatmap Pro start after permits or news; Pandell manages a client's own documents. None of them controls the recorder relationship. Title plants such as First American DataTree hold indexed documents for title workflows, not a cleaned cross-county alert feed. The county-software and digitization vendors (Tyler, Fidlar and Kofile appear to be the main ones, none verified here) are the real risk and might build the same thing. We differ by working on top of whichever system the county runs, by contracting with the county rather than the vendor, and by owning the entity graph. Enverus can add a feature but not a hundred county contracts.

title: Paid-But-Dark: Solar Loan Book Audit
one_liner: A fixed-fee audit and ongoing watch that tells credit unions, servicers and ABS holders which of their solar loans finance a roof that was never switched on. It then cures the worst ones through a supplier-neutral contractor bench.
customer: Wedge: chief credit or risk officers and loss-mitigation heads at mid-size credit unions and community banks that hold indirect solar loans originated through installer dealer networks. Second wave: servicers and ABS controlling-class investors that inherited books from failed platforms (Solar Servicing LLC-type). Deliberately not the seven Freedom Forever financiers, who already have ops teams and are already staffed. Start with legacy books from Titan, SunPower, Sunnova, PosiGen, and Mosaic- and Sunlight-financed loans.
problem: Loan tapes track payments, not power. Many dealer-channel programs released milestone money at 'installed', so a loan on a dark roof looks like ordinary credit stress and gets routed to collections, which is the wrong workout. The holder cannot tell installer-caused non-payment from real credit distress. Reserves are mis-sized and nobody in the institution owns the question 'is the system switched on?'. Judges flagged three weaknesses in the parent: the first wave is already staffed, paperwork-only jobs are price-pressured (Atma quotes up to about $1,200), and demand is lumpy.
solution: Step 1, a 10-day Book Audit. Ingest the loan tape (address, funding dates, installer ID, milestone dates). Cross-match it to county permit portals, public state interconnection datasets, borrower-authorized monitoring links and installer status. Output a loan-level tier: Energized, Dark-fixable, Dark-blocked-by-records, or Never-started. Add cost-to-cure, expected recovered loan value, and a one-page loss-reserve summary the CFO can hand to auditors. Step 2, a quarterly PTO-lag surveillance subscription on the whole book and on new originations, with installer-health flags, so nothing goes dark silently again. Step 3, cure orchestration at fixed prices by tier, using an open bench (Atma-type installers, Revival, ECG, Optimus, laid-off crews) and engineering subs. GreenLancer can be a supplier here. The paperwork-only tier is passed through at roughly the $1.2k benchmark plus a fixed coordination fee. The margin lives in the audit, the surveillance and the hard tiers (missing hardware, inspection fixes).
why_now: Freedom Forever went to Chapter 7 on Aug 7, 2026 (claims due Oct 16). It showed that lenders could not see which loans sat on dark roofs, and the same problem is buried in older Titan, SunPower, Sunnova and PosiGen books. The 25D credit ended for 2026 expenditures, so origination volume is down and more installer failures are likely. First-principles cost stack: reading messy permit files and utility portals used to cost $100+ of coordinator time per job. Document and browser agents now do it for a few dollars, so a per-loan audit can be priced below a credit union's discretionary-spend threshold at good margin.
revenue_model: Audit at $10-20 per loan with a $30k minimum (a 3,000-loan book is about $45-60k). Surveillance at $3-6 per loan per year. Cure coordination fee of $300 on paperwork-only jobs. A 20-30% markup on hard-tier cures ($3-8k each). A $500 PTO bonus. Later, licensing of per-AHJ and per-utility playbooks. Bottom-up: 60 institutions in 24 months at about $60k first-year value is about $3.6M before any cure revenue.
non_obvious_insight: The lender's blind spot is a missing column, not missing crews. Selling to the CFO or CRO's loss-reserve problem, instead of to a loss-mitigation desk waiting for the next bankruptcy, turns event-driven demand into continuous demand. Because the audit is a small fixed-fee purchase and not a vendor selection, it slips under procurement thresholds and creates its own list of jobs to cure. A finding of 'this roof is dark' changes the workout from collections to cure, which is where the loan value is recovered.
first_30_days: Week 1: hold 5 calls with credit union CROs and servicer COOs. Ask what they pay today, whether GreenLancer or anyone already covers them, and who owns the reserve question. This is the kill test: if GreenLancer's seven financiers already cover servicers and credit unions, downgrade. Weeks 1-3: build the screen on public data for one state that publishes interconnection records (California's DG Stats is the largest). Publish an anonymized ZIP-level 'permit-final-but-no-PTO' index for Titan and Freedom Forever-era permits as a lead magnet, with no homeowner addresses. Weeks 2-4: offer 3 credit unions a free NDA'd 300-loan scan with a paid full-book option. Recruit 2 ex-installer permit coordinators and sign 2 licensed subs. Goal: one signed paid audit within 60 days.

title: Orphan Lien Clearance Desk for Title Agents
one_liner: A flat-fee curative service that proves dead solar fixture filings and other zombie liens are dead (or gets them released) so home closings stop stalling.
customer: Independent title and escrow agencies and real estate attorneys in high-solar states (AZ, CA, FL, TX, NJ, NC, NV, CO), billed per file and usually paid by the seller at closing. Listing agents in solar-heavy markets are a second channel.
problem: Sunnova filed Chapter 11 in June 2025 (500,000+ customers), Mosaic and PosiGen followed, and the residential solar credit ended for 2026 installs, so thousands of homes carry UCC-1 fixture filings and recorded solar-lease notices held by dead, merged or reassigned entities. Title examiners flag every one. Agents can't tell who holds the debt now, whether the filing is even still legally effective, or how to get a termination, so closings slip days or weeks. The people currently serving this are consumer SEO and lead-gen sites, not the title agents who actually need it solved on a deadline.
solution: Per-file lien autopsy delivered in 48 hours. (1) Pull the recorded instrument and any continuation or termination filings from the county index and the Secretary of State. (2) Compute lapse under UCC 9-515 (five years unless continued in the six-month window). (3) Trace the assignment and servicer chain through bankruptcy dockets and servicer notices. (4) Deliver either an underwriter-ready 'lapsed, no exception' memo, or a payoff/estoppel request plus a pre-drafted termination (UCC-3, or debtor-filed termination where the statute allows) recorded in that county's required format. Recorded memoranda of lease, which do not lapse, get a release workflow instead. Later expand the same engine to satisfied-but-never-released mortgages, expired judgment liens, dead PACE liens and resurfaced zombie second mortgages.
why_now: 2025-2026 solar installer bankruptcies (Sunnova, Mosaic, PosiGen) and the end of the residential solar credit produced the largest single wave of orphaned fixture filings ever recorded. 2018-2021 installs are now hitting their five-year lapse dates just as those homes come to market. Title agents are short-staffed and want to outsource curative work, and an LLM can read county index entries and bankruptcy docket text cheaply.
revenue_model: Flat fee of about $395-$900 per cleared file, contingent on clear-to-close. Agencies with volume pay $299/month plus a reduced per-file rate. White-label API for underwriters and closing software later.
non_obvious_insight: Half the 'problem liens' in solar-heavy counties are already legally dead, but the county index never shows lapse, so examiners treat a 2019 fixture filing as live forever. Clerks watch continuation filings come in, and most small installers never filed one. The work is proof of death, not payoff. Insiders also know the recorded 'notice of lease' is a different animal that never lapses, and that a clerk must record a debtor-filed termination on its face, since the office is ministerial.
first_30_days: Offer the first five files free to 3-5 independent title agencies in Phoenix, Tampa and Sacramento. Build the lapse calculator and county-index lookups for about 10 counties. Get one regional agent underwriter to accept a standard lapse-memo format. Then price at $495 per file and ask each agency for a testimonial and two referrals to listing agents.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SunStrong Management (successor servicer for the Sunnova book), Wolters Kluwer Lien Solutions / CSC (UCC search, filing, continuation and termination vendors), Qualia (title/escrow closing platform), Nationwide Title Clearing / national title-clearing and lien-release outsourcers (ServiceLink, etc.). White space: Research limits: the session's WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was exhausted, so I ran no searches. I used direct fetches of known URLs (Wikipedia, Cornell LII for the UCC text, SunStrong, Sunnova, Qualia, TitleCapture, Simplifile, the YC directory) and a GitHub repo search. Several guessed URLs 404'd or returned 403. Competitor coverage is therefore thin, and I found no funded startup doing solar-specific lien-lapse analysis and curative for title agents. Absence in my results is weak evidence, not proof.

Unserved as far as I could tell: a title-agent-facing, per-file workflow that (a) classifies the instrument (UCC-1 fixture filing vs. SOS-only filing vs. recorded memorandum or notice of lease vs. PACE vs. mortgage), (b) computes lapse under UCC 9-515, and (c) routes the file to the current servicer with a pre-formatted payoff, estoppel or UCC-3 request. Incumbent UCC vendors and general title-clearing outsourcers do not appear to package this for solar.

Substantive weaknesses to weigh against the gap:
- Lapse is not death. Cornell LII (https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/9/9-515) confirms that on lapse the interest becomes unperfected, and is deemed never perfected only as against a purchaser for value. The debt and the interest against the debtor survive. In a lease or PPA the lessor owns the equipment, so a lapse memo does not clear ownership or the lease. The buyer still needs an assumption or buyout. Underwriters may therefore refuse to rely on 'lapsed, no exception' memos, and getting one to accept a format is the make-or-break step.
- Debtor-filed terminations are narrow. UCC 9-509(d)(2) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/9/9-509) requires the secured party to have failed to comply with 9-513, plus debtor authorization and a statement on the form. That generally means a demand and a wait, and it only works where no obligation is still secured. That conflicts with a 48-hour SLA.
- The 'orphan' premise is overstated for Sunnova, the biggest name. Its assets went to new owners and SunStrong runs a home-sale transfer process. The truly orphaned pool (Mosaic, PosiGen, small defunct installers) is smaller and messier. Sunnova is confirmed only via Wikipedia and the SunStrong and Sunnova sites. I could not fetch a Mosaic or PosiGen page.
- Unauthorized-practice-of-law exposure for underwriter-facing lapse opinions unless an attorney of record signs.
- Per-county recording quirks make it operations-heavy, not pure software.

title: Big-Meter Replacement Fund, Repaid by Verified Uplift
one_liner: A meter-brand-neutral fund buys, installs and owns a utility's worst large meters at zero upfront cost. The utility repays 70% of measured incremental revenue for up to 5 years, with an open verification protocol that makes it an underwritable asset class.
customer: Utilities with 5k-100k connections that know their big meters are old but have no capex or staff. That is most utilities carrying PFAS and lead-line programs. The wedge buyer is a city or district finance director who can sign a no-cost, contingent-payment services contract under their small-purchase limit. Later, infrastructure lenders and the SRF or muni-lease programs that co-finance the fund.
problem: Replacing a large meter is a financing problem, not an information problem. A top-quartile large meter (3-10 inch) costs about $5-25k installed and can recover $6-15k a year in missed water and sewer revenue, which is a payback of about 1-2 years. Yet it stays unfunded. The benefit lands in the revenue line that nobody budgets as upside, while the cost hits scarce capex competing with lead lines and PFAS treatment. Council needs a procurement, an appropriation and a crew. An audit like the sharpened version tells them what to fix, but leaves them to fund and execute it. ESCOs bundle it into large projects with the vendor's own hardware, and meter vendors finance only their own meters.
solution: Underwrite: the screen ranks candidate meters by expected uplift and only meters with payback under about 2 years enter the fund. Verify: an open measurement and verification protocol (pre-swap on-site accuracy test at three flow rates, post-swap test, then 12 months of billing versus matched peer accounts) in the style of IPMVP for energy. Fund: the fund buys meters through distributors at volume and pays independent plumbers and a test subcontractor for the swap. Repay: the utility pays a metering-service fee of 70% of verified incremental revenue per meter, for up to 60 months or until 1.8x of capital is returned, never more, then owns the meter. Payments are contingent, not debt, and recovery is prospective, so no back-billing. Every swap adds a before-and-after label to the yield model, which lowers the cost of capital. Later, pool contracts and sell them to infrastructure debt or bank warehouse lines.
why_now: Revenue-backed, measured-savings financing has already worked for solar PPAs and energy performance contracts once a standard M&V existed. Water meters have none. Utilities are capital-starved by PFAS and lead-line mandates and need off-balance-sheet fixes. AMI interval data makes before-and-after verification cheap enough to sell to lenders. Data engineering means a small team can build the underwriting model, and distributors are eager to move meter volume.
revenue_model: Return on deployed capital: assumed 25-30% net unlevered (about $9k average installed cost, about $6k a year of measured uplift, 70% share, 2-2.5x lifetime multiple, less yield and dispute losses). Fees: 3-5% origination and a verification fee per meter. Later: a warehouse line then securitization of the contract pool. Data licensing of the accuracy-by-model-and-age dataset to lenders, consultants and vendors. Start-up capital: a $250-400k first pilot from angels or a revenue-based lender, plus extended payment terms from a meter distributor.
non_obvious_insight: An accurate large meter is a small, measurable cash-producing asset with almost no credit risk, because its yield, not the city's credit, pays it back. What is missing is a trusted way to measure the yield. Whoever writes and owns the verification protocol and holds the labeled before-and-after data has a standard-setter's position and a compounding cost-of-capital advantage: each verified swap makes the next loan cheaper. Meter distributors are suppliers and floor-plan lenders here, not enemies, because the fund is a volume buyer that creates demand they cannot create.
first_30_days: Write v0.1 of the verification protocol as a 2-page public document and get two reviewers: a water-loss practitioner and a municipal attorney (to review the contingent service-contract form and the state's non-appropriation rules). Get 90-180 day terms from two distributors on 25 large meters and a rate for a test-rig subcontractor. Run free top-100 scans for 6 utilities of 10-40k connections and pick the one with the best yield and a cooperative finance director. Propose a no-cost 25-meter pilot with 70% of verified uplift for 60 months. Line up the first $250-400k. Aim to have the pilot contract on a council agenda inside 90 days.
lineage: mutation of I0388 ('Contingency Hunters for Unbilled Water Revenue'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Itron (Temetra Analysis / Non-Revenue Water portfolio), Badger Meter (BEACON, OneNetwork), Master Meter (Harmony Encore MDM), Metron-Farnier (WaterScope). White space: Important caveat: my WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) before any of my searches ran. This verdict rests on about 20 direct page fetches and GitHub repo searches, not on broad web, Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt sweeps. Treat 'no direct competitor found' as unconfirmed, and do a manual pass on Crunchbase, YC and RFP portals before committing. What I did verify: (1) I found no vendor selling a contingency-fee service that joins assessor roll, footprints, imagery and the billing system to produce named unbilled addresses for water utilities. (2) The metering and analytics incumbents (Itron, Badger, Master Meter, Metron) sell software tied to their own hardware, with no evidence of a ranked, dollar-denominated, legal-ready recovery list or contingency pricing. (3) The GitHub search for open-source tools found nothing relevant.
